speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM WITH RESPECT TO COMPANY'S LABOUR POLICY
speechtext:
I think I should direct attention to the fact that a few days ago the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) made a statement regarding labour conditions, and the attention of the president of the British American Oil Company, Limited, having been directed to his statement, quoting a statement which appeared in a newspaper not published in Canada, a memorandum was sent to me which reads as follows:
On page 3465 of Hansard, July 7th, are remarks dealing with the labour policy of The British American Oil Company Limited. These remarks are misleading and untrue.
The construction of the refinery at Montreal is, in the main, under contract to various firms, and such work as is being performed by the company is being paid for at rates prevailing for similar work in the city of Montreal.
No labour organization, or individual, for that matter, has made complaint to the company as to rates of wages being paid according to testimony of the Montreal office of the company.
The policy of the company has, since its incorporation in 1906, been very favourable to labour.
Employees, after two years' service have their lives insured in favour of their estate, or such beneficiary as they may name, the total expense being borne by the company; this insurance continued in force so long as the worker remains in the employ of the company.
The company contributes 50 per cent (the employees the balance), to a sick benefit fund which gives employees income during illness and carries with it payments in connection with funeral expenses to worker or any member of his family.
The present rates of wages are not below those effective during the war period, or subsequent thereto.
Employees have a works committee which meets with management, and never once has there been a demand for increased wages, and consequently there has never been a strike in any of the company's plants.
It is significant that the subject matter to which reference is made appeared in a United States labour publication, namely "Labor." Washington, D.C., June 30, 1931. If there were foundation for the charges then, why did not one, at least, if not all, of the Canadian labour papers deal with the matter? Canadian labour is not unmindful of the fact that through the construction of refinery at Montreal The

Business of the House
British American Oil Company is contributing in this item alone over $1,000,000 directly to the workers.
Mr. Heenan mentions The Toronto Iron Works Limited as a close ally of The British American Oil Company. There is no connection between The Toronto Iron Works and The British American Oil Company. A. L. Ellsworth, the president of both companies, established The British American Oil Company in 1906, and The Toronto Iron Works in 1907. While A. L. Ellsworth and P. W. Binns are officers of both companies, yet they are inactive in The Toronto Iron Works Limited, and the companies have no community of interest through stock ownership.
The Toronto Iron Works Limited has done much work over the past years in the eastern provinces, including Quebec, and is paying today rates of wages at Montreal no lower than paid in the past. The maximum rate is 83 cents per hour, and the minimum rate for unskilled labour is 35 cents per hour.
The company, in common with most contractors, employs its men nine hours per day.
No Sunday work.
There is not one iota of excuse for the use of the words, "bludgeoning, bullying and discriminating," as used by Mr. Heenan based upon the matter contained in the Washington publication.
I make no comment on this memorandum in any way, shape or form, but I think in all fairness I must, as minister, communicate it to the 'house in the same sense in which it was forwarded to me by the president of the company concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose last night it was considering item No. 55 of the schedule. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, when
we were speaking about corn last night I referred to the fact that the western grain growers would like to have cheaper freight rates for grain and fodder so that their coarse grains may be shipped at lower rates to the markets throughout Canada. I wish to substantiate what I said by reading an extract from a publication by the National Dairy Council of Canada following its meeting of March, 1931. On page 76 I find the following:
Cheaper feeds are.essential if there is to be an expanding production of dairy products. These are attainable through:-
(a) Cheaper distribution of grains and mill feeds. This involves lower freight rate to the extreme eastern and western parts of Canada in addition to bulk shipments and storage. The operations of the coarse grain pool promise to materially assist in this regard.
In other words the National Dairy Council is urging that there should be cheaper freight rates for coarse grain. I maintained last night and repeat to-day that the proposed duty on com will mean added expense to those people who are carrying on the dairy industry, trying to fatten cattle or to raise poultry. My suggestion to the Prime

Minister would be to leave the duty on corn as it is, namely, to leave it free for feeding purposes. As he has seen fit to allow a five cent freight rate on wheat I would suggest that he should make the same rate applicable to barley and coarse grains for domestic feeding purposes in order that the farmers in eastern Canada may be able to obtain barley at a cheaper rate. Either he should do that or cut the freight rates. It is absolutely essential however, if we are going to continue as a dairy producing and mixed farming country, that we should have our feeds distributed at cheaper rates throughout the Dominion. Either our farmers in western Canada must have assistance to bring their coarse grains at cheaper rates 'to eastern Canada and into British Columbia or assistance must be given either through cheaper freight rates or by the five cents which is being given to the wheat growers. In my opinion that should apply also to the barley growers so that their coarse grains may be delivered at cheaper rates. I should like to know whether or not the Prime Miinster will take into consideration the wishes of the National Dairy Council and the farmers throughout Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Freight rates will not be dealt with by this legislation, because the government does not make them. They are made by the Board of Railway Commissioners. In my view the matters referred to by my hon. friend are not relevant on these tariff items. The remarks of my hon. friend with respect to freight rates have been repeated frequently, and sometimes I wonder whether hon. members realize the deficits with which the railways are faced at the present time and where those railway companies will find themselves if such deficits continue.
What about five cents a bushel?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is to help the wheat growers.	[DOT]

If I may be permitted to say so, about the only way that coarse grains from the western provinces can be brought to the maritimes is by some change in the freight rates. A couple of years ago I thought I had made a good case concerning mill feeds and course grains before the railway commission on behalf of the farmers of eastern Canada. Despite that fact however we received no reduction and no benefit. The condition of maritime farmers in regard to mill feeds and coarse grains is this: The

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
farmers of Denmark and other European countries can procure their feeds cheaper than the farmers of the maritime provinces. I would like the Prime Minister to say whether or not he thinks that is fair either to the producers of coarse grains in western Canada or the farmers in the maritimes. The export rate on grain and mill feeds is so low that they can be brought to the seaports in the maritimes, shipped to Europe and our friends in Denmark can get their feed cheaper than we can. That is the competition we have to meet on the markets of the world. I do not think any government in Canada should tolerate such conditions as that. Canadian farmers should be .given a fair chance with the farmers of other parts of the world. If the party in power is a Canada-first party I think they should endeavour to see that all parts of Canada are treated fairly in this matter. I have no objection to five cents on wheat for export, but I think it should apply to coarse grains as well so that bran and millfeeds may be brought more cheaply to the farmers of the maritimes. As to the duty on corn increasing the sale of coarse grains in the maritime provinces, I do not think it will have this effect unless there is a revision of the freight rates. The fox ranches of Prince Edward Island use large quantities of corn meal, and if the price of furs continues to drop we may have to resort more than ever to corn meal, as it is the cheapest feed available. I understand the corn is imported and ground in Canada and shipped all over the Dominion.
Educate them to eat barley.

I do not think there would be any chance in the world of the prairie provinces finding a market for their barley in Prince Edward Island, for our farmers already grow enough of this grain for their own use. I understand that the barley crop is not as large in Nova Scotia as it is in Prince Edward Island, and consequently there is a larger market there for the sale of barley than in my province. The only grain we bring in is corn, and naturally we would be opposed to the imposition of this duty.

Mr. Chairman, while I have no intention whatever of holding up this item, I wish to make another appeal to the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) to allow corn for feeding purposes to come in free of duty. When the committee rose last night I was saying that in my boyhood days I had been brought up
at the feet of such men as Doctor James Mills, Professor Panton and Professor Day- men who did so much to make the Ontario Agricultural college and experimental farm the famous institution that it is to-day, for its reputation extends throughout the world. I have under my hand a pamphlet issued by the animal husbandry division of the dominion experimental farm which strongly advises the feeding of barley to our stock.

How about a little
barley corn?

It will take
me just that much longer if my hon. friends of the opposition wish to interrupt.

We are not on
the opposition side.

Although my
friends are sitting on the government side they are in opposition to what I am saying at the present time. I would remind the committee that the men who direct the Ontario Agricultural college would not think of publishing a bulletin unless it were based on experiments carefully conducted over a period of years. May I call the attention of older members of the committee to a fact, which no doubt they will recall, that a certain variety of two-rowed barley was given to the farmers all over Ontario to test out on experimental plots. In those days I was conducting experiments on my father's farm. We experimented with that grain for four successive years and then considered it sufficiently good to recommend it to our fellow farmers. The second year, however, we found that grain was a dead failure, and I may add that after four or five years' further experiments by many farmers in Ontario as well as by the Ontario Agricultural college, that grain went out of use much more rapidly than it came in. In the light of that experience I am strongly of the opinion that a bulletin such as this should not be distributed until the experiments in the use of barley as a feed for stock had been conducted over a sufficiently long period to remove all doubt regarding its merits as a stock food ration. I notice a section of this bulletin headed Barley as a Feed for Horses. Let me quote:
Another reason is the general impression that barley is 'a dangerous grain for horses, in that its use is frequently conducive to a scurfy condition of the skin and to itching, scurfy legs, 

"too heating," the horseman says. Possibly a third reason is the comparative lack of palatability of barley compared with oats.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
So far as the section comprising Ontario and eastern Canada is concerned, I am satisfied that barley in its raw state is a dangerous feed for our horses; boiled it is much more palatable and safe; although I do believe from information I have received that barley may safely be fed to horses in the United States on the Pacific slope. But for our dairy cattle and young growing animals, it is a grain which no one with any experience would recommend except as forming a very small percentage of the ration.
Speaking from my own experience and in view of the fact that corn is eagerly sought after by the farmers of the western section of Ontario, particularly in my own county, I would plead again with tlhe Minister of Finance to allow this grain to come in free. I ask him to allow the farmers of Ontario to use their own judgment. They will not bring in corn if they do not think it pays them to do so. As I said last night, it was only after they had agitated for years that corn be put on the free list for feeding purposes that the government of that day, some 'thirty-five years ago, saw fit eventually to do so, and from that day to this corn has been allowed to remain on the free list. As my la^t word I would urge the Minister o'f Finance to allow corn to remain on the free list and so permit our farmers to exercise their own judgment as to whether they will purchase this grain or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should be sorry to think that this was the last word of the hon. gentleman-
On the matter of corn.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Oh,-or would I be deprived of a very great pleasure. I think I forgot to say to the hon. members for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), and Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) that South African corn, which is now a very important factor in the world's production, will come in free, and therefore reach the ports of Halifax and Vancouver as heretofore under the British preference. I should also state, what possibly is fairly well known to some hon. gentlemen, that there was a time when we produced 15,000,000 bushels of corn, but the advent into this country of the oorn-borer reduced our production to less than
5.000. 000.	Last year it was approximately
6.000.	000 bushels. It was said last evening by the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott) that it is believed the production will reach
10.000.	000 or 12,000,000 bushels this year, and the area is being increased by thousands of
|Mr. T. 'McMillan.]
acres during the present season. It is not improbable therefore that to some considerable extent the requirements of Ontario will be met by Ontario production, but to the extent to which it is not in other parts of Canada, having regard as I pointed out to transportation costs, there will be the opportunity for the use of Coarse grains which will not bear the cost of export. Under these circumstances I do not know that I can add anything to the very laudable desire of the hon. gentleman, whose ripe experience and rich fund of humour contribute so greatly to the happiness of the government.

I do not wish to prolong the debate, but I am anxious to relieve the mind of the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan). Last night the hon. gentleman spoke of getting Essex corn in his boyhood days, which would not keep because of the moisture content. In recent years Essex and Kent counties have been carrying on experiments, and now are growing a very high grade of corn, which is only 10 per cent greater in moisture content than Kansas corn, which is supposed to be the hardest and dryest corn on the continent. So I do not think the hon. member for South Huron should worry over a corn famine in Huron county because of this duty, since the county of Essex will be able to take care of their requirements, either by shiploads or carloads. In past years Essex county has shipped thousands of cars of corn to all parts of western Ontario, and personally I have never heard any complaint with regard to its quality. It is not the fault of the government if a shipment happens to be too moist; that is the fault of the inspector who ships the corn. I believe the 25 cents a bushel duty will 'help the farmers of Essex, Kent and Elgin counties very materially, since corn is one of the most profitable crops they can grow, therefore, I am heartily in favour of the proposed rate of duty.

If the Prime Minister makes another speech probably he will shatter completely the hopes of the farmers of the west. Last night when he indicated that under the treaty with the Argentine corn would come in at 18 cents instead of 25 cents I thought I saw a look of dismay come over the faces of some of my hon, friends from Manitoba. Now he tells us that corn may come in from South Africa free, so I think the hopes of the farmers of Manitoba will be down 100 per cent by now.
I am not going to discuss this matter from the standpoint of the "dietetic eccentricities"

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
of a chicken-and if Hansard will put those words in quotation marks I will not be robbing my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Willis) of that very choice phrase-but I do wish to discuss it from the standpoint of common sense. Before coming to this house, and since I have been here, I never pleaded for protection on any farm products, and I do not intend to begin now. In my judgment the farmer who links himself up with the principle of protection completely destroys his own position when seeking relief from the burdens which the protective system imposes upon him. I can well understand the attitude of some of the hon. gentlemen from the west, and in a measure I sympathize with them. They realize that they must go home carrying very little in the way of spoils and with very little to show in the way of the fulfilment of the promises made during the last election, so they are very anxious to have this little bit of a duty on com which, in my judgment, really will amount to nothing as far as the western farmer is concerned.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Is he opposed to this duty on corn; yes or no? Do not hedge, now; what is the answer?

That is a question I do
not object to answering, but before doing so I should like to ask another question of hon. members opposite; if I answer questions they should be willing to answer questions also. Before answering that question I should like to ask hon. gentlemen from the prairies if they are in favour of the 25 per cent duty on agricultural implements; if they are in favour of what has been done in regard to the raw material for the manufacture of binder twine; if they are in favour of what has been done in regard to barbed wire and a host of other things. I can put questions to hon. gentlemen opposite which will be just as embarrassing as questions they may put to me. I am going to answer that question, and I can do it with no embarrassment at all. I am opposed to the whole policy of this government in regard to tariffs. I am opposed to a duty on corn for the reason that I do not propose to hamstring myself when I come to advocate a reduction of the duty on those things which I use. In my judgment this proposition to put a duty on corn will be of very little, if any, advantage to the grower of western grain. When hon. gentlemen opposite from the prairies will answer the questions I have put to them as candidly as I have answered their question, we will have an interesting exhibition in this house.

Will the hon. gentleman
permit me to answer his question? We gave a pledge to the electors in that country that we would support protection as long as the prices were not raised. [DOT] The prices of machinery and all other commodities have gone down under the policy of the right hon. Minister of Finance.

I said I could sympathize
with hon. gentlemen opposite. They know they must go home with very little to show in fulfilment of the promises they made during the last election, so they want to carry home this little duty on com and the five cent rate on wheat.
Are you in favour of that?

That is another question
of the same kind. I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that what they will have to show their constituents as a result of their labours will be but as dust in the balance compared with the duty on agricultural implements, the imposition in regard to barbed wire, the action of the government in regard to the raw materials entering into the production of binder twine, and a host of other things. For my part I am going to take good care that the eyes of the farmers are not blinded by these little things to the neglect of the many more important things in this budget.

I should like to add just a
few words to what has been said with regard to corn. Last night the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) spoke on this matter and opposed the duty on corn. I am from the eastern portion of the same county, and I wish to say that I am decidedly in favour of the duty. Our people in the county of Middlesex can raise corn in abundance, and I am sure that they will strongly favour this duty. I believe the farmers of our country should receive protection on a great many commodities, and the duty on corn is one of the ways in which we can protect our farmers to some extent.

As one of
the members from the eastern part of Saskatchewan I think it is my duty to make just a few observations as to my position with respect to this duty. During the campaign last year one of the issues was the placing of

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
a duty on corn and it met with favour. I have had many letters from my electors and they are very much in favour of the government's action in placing a duty on corn. In the eastern part of Saskatchewan we have been growing more and more barley, and, as the hon. member for Souris said last night, we have great quantities of this grain in storage.	[DOT]
As regards the comparative feed value of barley and corn, I do not think it is necessary to say anything further. Statistics have been given, and the hon. member for Souris in his first apeecih made a very good case in favour of barley. At any rate, the difference, if any, is so slight that it is not worth considering. Practical feeding tests have proven that you can get as large a percentage of gain on the average animal with barley as with corn. With respect to the feeding of poultry, a good deal was said in the house last night, and I would direct attention to the evidence given before the committee on agriculture [DOT] on June 9 by Mr. Brown, chief of the poultry division of the Department of Agriculture, in which he stated that eggs from the western provinces had a premium in the Montreal market. He stated further that prairie extras on the Montreal market were a product to be proud of. At the present time hens in the west are not being fed com.
I with to refer to a point that has not yet been discussed in this house with reference to corn. I think hon. members will agree with me that the area in which corn is produced on the North American continent is gradually extending north. I think it was three years ago-the ex-Minidter of Agriculture will bear me out-that we held a corn show in the town of Indian Head. We showed corn that was produced in all parts of the western provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and the exhibition proved conclusively that corn grown in the prairie provinces is equal in qualty to any com produced in the states to the south of us. A representative from that com area in the United States attended the show and he said that our corn was of equal quality with any corn grown in the United States. This spring farmers have had inquiries for com grown in the western provinces for seeding purposes in the states south of us as far as Texas.
I venture to say that under normal climatic conditions we can produce a large quantity of good corn in western Canada. It would not take a very great amount of corn to supply even the demand for feeding purposes. Take British Columbia, for instance: two hundred thousand acres of corn would supply 
the demand. Under favourable climatic conditions, therefore, that industry could be developed right in our own country so that there would be no need for us to worry about corn coming from other parts of the world.
It has been suggested on the other side that it would be better to have a reduction in freight rates. I think the placing of a duty on corn is a very good argument in favour of an adjustment of domestic freight rates, and it would appear to be necessary. And if the extreme east and west would come in on it, that would be a great argument in support of such an adjustment. I am surprised to observe that many hon. members on the opposite side from the western provinces are quibbling on this question. They are trying to justify their opposition to the duty on corn. When their electors read the speeches they have been making on this question the impression will not be very favourable to them.
I am delighted to note the veiy ready response we have had on this side of the house from the extreme eastern and western members in supporting us with regard to this duty on corn. It is gratifying to see such a splendid spirit of national cooperation among the eastern and western members in this respect, and I am only too pleased to endorse and support the action of the government in placing the duty on corn.

I think we are all agreed that the government is desirous of helping someone, presumably the barley growers. Now, however, we find it is the corn growers whom this duty is intended to help-maybe both. At all events, it will put up the price of com. That is obvious. If you put on a duty of 25 cents a bushel, does anyone suggest that the result will not be an increase in price? I say it will put up the price; it will compel the buyers of corn to pay that much more for this commodity. And that will adversely affect the poultry industry. Now, the question is, what additional price will it require to move barley from western Canada either to the Pacific or down here? It cannot move itself; it will not pay for its carriage. The result is that a good deal of it is still on the farms. Low grade barley will have to be raised from 10 to 12 cents before it can begin to move. Will this duty on corn raise the price of barley 10 cents? If it does not, then the object of this duty will not be realized. You must get the barley to move, and it is not moving because of the low price. A good deal of

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
low grade barley and low grade wheat did not carry itself to Fort William, and the farmer had not only to give the barley away for the freight rate, but he was even billed by the railways for more. He was minus some dollars for freight besides giving away his barley or his wheat. I say, therefore, that this assistance, with all due respect to the Prime Minister in his desire to help the barley growers, will be ineffective unless it extends sufficient help to get the barley moving. And that will take 10 cents a bushel. Again I ask, will a duty of 25 cents on imported corn raise the price of barley 10 cents? I do not believe it will raise it one iota. It may give a market for the best barley, the kind of grain that will carry itself, to the extent of four million or five million bushels if that much corn is shut out by this 25 cents duty. But I do not know whether it will do that. One thing is dead sure, however: it is going to hurt the poultry growers. They will have to cough up more for their corn. To talk about barley being a substitute for corn in the feeding of poultry is absolute nonsense; you cannot get the poultrymen anywhere, in the east or in the west, to support such a contention. Ask the poultry themselves by throwing a mixture of corn, wheat, barley and oats before poultry and see which they will take first. They will take first the corn and next the wheat and then either the oats or barley depending upon which is the better quality. Poultry do not like barley in the whole state. I have a friend in Hamilton who is a manufacturer of high class poultry feeds. I am told by the best authorities that just to the extent that barley is substituted for corn, thus increasing the fibre content of the mixture, there must be added a quantity of hulled oats in order to keep down the fibre content. Not only that, but those mysterious vitamins of which we hear so much are lost. If barley is fed you must make up for the absence of the vitamins by the use of cod liver oil. Hon. members should not laugh at that, because that is the fact. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) referred to the duck farm at Knowlton. I had the pleasure of visiting this farm and one would think the whole top of the earth was a moving mass of ducks. The primary purpose of a duck is to be eaten. Enough eggs must be laid of course in order to perpetuate the species but the primary object is meat production. A duck is not very particular as to the palatability of its food; it will eat anything and that is one of the reasons why barley is used to the extent it is at the Knowlton farm.

They do
not need cod liver oil.

I understand that
for the first three or four years this Knowi-ton farm was a failure because of an insufficient number of ducks. They had to get the quantity up and the cost of feed down, and I believe they have reached that point to-day and for some years past and are making a great success. This is an entirely different thing to feeding hens for egg-laying purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will do me the kindness of recalling what I said when I brought down the budget, mow some weeks ago, he will recall that I gave the Argentine treaty as an illustration of an old British treaty.

I fail to see how this new tax on corn is going to help the farmers. Of course, we were told during the campaign that if the Conservatives were put into power the farmers would receive every consideration, but up to now I do not see how this government has helped the farmers in any way. Most of the poultry men, on the contrary, will suffer because of this increased tariff of 25 per cent on incubators for hatching eggs and on brooders for rearing young chickens, and complete parts of such equipment. I shall not be as prudent as the Postmaster General. I want to express myself very clearly on this question. I agree entirely with the ex-Minister of Agriculture when he says that this tax on corn cannot help the poultry men in eastern Canada at least. I am surprised that barley as a substitute for corn is at all palatable to the members sitting on the government side of the house. I think it is really more palatable to them than it is to the hens. I was also very much surprised a't the efforts of professional men in the house to convince the hen that barley was good for her. Thy may succeed in convincing their electors that barley is a good substitute for corn, but as a poultry man myself I challenge any one of them to make a trial of this substitute. In confirmation of this, let me quote from a very valuable bulletin published by the Department of Agriculture, under the genial direction of the Hon. Robert Weir, B.A., Minister of Agriculture, and of Dr. Archibald, director of the Dominion Experimental Farms. I quote from Seasonable Hints from the Dominion experimental farms, in its issue for the summer of 1931. It says:
Owing to its extremely low price barley is making up a greater part of the ration than ever before. At the present time it is more satisfactory ground and incorporated in the mash mixture rather than in the scratch grain owing to the fact that it is not very palatable to poultry.
Note that: It is not very palatable to poultry. I hope some hon. gentlemen will read this statement, which is published by the Department of Agriculture, before making
all sorts of statements in this house. It goes on:
That this lack of palatability is due to the hull-
It is not often that a lack of palatability is due to Hull:
-has been demonstrated at this division, where some machine-hulled barley has been used in an experimentental way with excellent results.
But note what follows:
Providing that the cost of hulling can be lowered sufficiently, hulled barley becomes the logical form in which to feed that grain in the scratch grain mixture.
But it has not been demonstrated that the cost of hulling barley can be lowered.
We have other instances of the sort of action this government is taking. They raised the tariff all around before establishing a tariff board. They raised the tariff on glass, for instance, before they knew what was coming. Now they have raised the tariff on corn, to encourage the use of barley as a substitute for corn, and as I have just shown by the quotation from the bulletin issued by the Department of Agriculture, barley as a substitute for corn for feeding hens is still in the experimental stage. I wonder if the very learned Minister of Agriculture has been consulted about this matter.
But the bulletin, after dealing with the lack of palatability of barley, goes on to say:
Barley may be substituted for corn in both scratch grain and mash mixtures providing that its deficiency in vitamin A be made up through the addition of good quality alfalfa leaf meal, green cut clover or alfalfa and cod liver oil to the ration.
Alfalfa is not grown to a very great extent in the province of Quebec. Its cultivation is, in fact, barely beyond the experimental stage, but I think there is a big future for alfalfa in the province of Quebec. It is recommended in this bulletin that there be added to the ration alfalfa leaf meal, green cut clover, or alfalfa and cod liver oil. I do not know if there is a tariff on cod liver oil. If not, it must have been forgotten and will no doubt be remembered next time.
I really fail to see how the farmers have been helped by this government. I remember distinctly my opponent in the last election, a very genial orator-it is my privilege always to have good opponents-promising that if the Conservatives got into power the price of butter would rise. But what is the price of butter to-day? It is all right to have the home market, but we are in the export market, and we will remain in the export market for a long

while. What is the price of eggs? May I say that if the farmers as a last resort were able to sell a few dozen eggs at a good price they would be assured of at least a little cash. The government proposes to increase the price of corn by 25 cents a bushel. Unless the good Tories succeed in educating the hens I am very much afraid we will not be able to substitute barley for corn, because particularly in the winter time such a substitution would be impossible. On many occasions I have tried it, and as for nine years I have been president of the poultry association in the province from which I come I think I ought to know something about the matter. In different contests I have received many prizes for my hens, and have taken an interest in poultry raising. I fail to see in this instance what good the government is doing.
Later on when we reach the subject of wool I shall have something further to say because I believe that is the only commodity in connection with which a tariff will give an advantage to the farmers. Certainly it has not given any advantage so far as butter, eggs and grain are concerned. Now the poultry men are faced with this impediment, and I think I am voicing the view's of the poultry men of the province of Quebec when I register my opposition to the proposed tariff on corn.

To my mind it is rather
amusing that some hon. members opposite should find fault with the action of the government when it tends to increase the price of farm products. For about three months we have listened to speeches from hon. members on both sides of the house and most of them have dealt with the depression with which this country is now faced. In the main I think the economic condition may be traced to the lack of purchasing power of Canadian farmers. Surely any steps taken by this government to increase that purchasing power should be in the interests not only of Canadian farmers but of Canadians as a whole.
I hope the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) will not misjudge my remarks when I say that I have been unable to follow the force of his argument. He has said that he is opposed to the proposed tariff because it will increase the price of farm products, and that among other things it will increase the price of corn. Hon. members have said that large quantities of corn are grown in Canada, and that when a demand is made more will be grown. If we wish to place the farmers in a purchasing position w-e must give them something more than the bare cost of production. One of the first acts of this

government was to introduce legislation to increase the price of farm products, but strange to say that action has met with severe criticism by hon. members opposite. The ex-Minister of Agriculture has said that the price of corn will be increased, and that therefore the price of that commodity grown by Canadian producers will also increase. He has admitted further that to some extent, at least, the price of barley will increase.
No.

I thought my hon. friend
said that.
No.

I think it is evident that the price of barley will be increased. Let us suppose however that the price of that commodity does not go up and look at the matter from a different viewpoint. At present there are 100,000,000 bushels of barley in storage waiting for a market. If a feed market can be secured whereby the poultry producers and stock feeders of Canada will feed barley instead of corn surely the producers will be in a position to dispose of great quantities in storage. In western Canada money will be placed in circulation and the farmers will be in a position to make purchases, resulting in great benefit to Canada as a whole. To my mind that is a logical argument.
I would ask hon. members to place themselves in the position of the farmers in western Canada who have millions of bushels of barley in storage which they cannot sell. Their first thought is to find a market for their product and this government has taken a step which will secure a market for at least a portion of that great amount in storage. For that action I think the government is to be commended.
Something has been said concerning the palatability of barley. I do not wish to take up the time of the house in dealing further with that matter, but I wish to ask hon. members on both sides of the house who enjoy their fall shooting where they find the wild ducks? If hon. members wish to go out for a stubble shoot where do they go? Do they go to the wheat stubble; do they go to the oat stubble?-no, they go to the barley stubble. That is where they find the game, and as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said, "You cannot fool a hen." Likewise, you cannot fool a duck. There they are to be found in their wild state, and they pick out barley every time upon which to feed.

speechtext: In 1930, 168,200 hundredweight, valued at $565,000. Seventy-one thousand hundredweight came from Hong Kong and 56,000 hundredweight from the United States.

I want to draw the attention of the committee to the way in which the customs regulations work out, but not for the purpose of blaming the government, because it happened before this government came into power. Rice grown in British Burma used to fee shipped to Holland and there the hulls were removed; then it was shipped to Canada. The importers claimed it should be admitted to Canada under the intermediate rate because we had a treaty with Holland, but the customs officials said, "No, there is not sufficient Dutch labour in it to qualify under the intermediate tariff." "Very well," said the importers, "if this is not Holland rice it must be British rice"-it came from British Burma -"and therefore it should enter unden the British preference." "No," said the customs officials, "once this rice left British Burma and entered Holland it lost its nationality and now it cannot come in as British rice, nor can it come in as Dutch rice; it is rice without a country." As I said, I am not attaching any blame to the government in this case, but I just wanted to draw attention to the fact that our customs regulations are such that sometimes we get the most ridiculous rulings. Here is rice that ordinarily might come in under the intermediate tariff, but being denied that rate is not allowed to be admitted as British rice under the British preferential rate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I happen to know the case to which the hon. gentleman refers and I did make inquiries with respect to it. The answer which I received at that time seemed to me to be a fairly good answer:	It is not
British rice because it did not come direct from a British possession to Canada, therefore it is not British for customs purposes. There was not sufficient labour of the country from whence it came to entitle it to the intermediate. It is not a question of nationality, it is a question of its being entitled to the benefit of certain tariff provisions. I have not yet been able to see that the answer given to me is not a fairly good one. The statutory requirement with respect to British rice is that it must come direct to qualify as such.

How would that explanation fit in with the provision we have in the

West Indian treaty, that where goods come direct to Canadian ports we give them a ten per cent reduction? Surely if that is a sound principle, then-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon.
member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) did not follow me. Had the rice come direct from British Burma to a Canadian port and the rate had been in excess of fifty cents, there would have been a reduction of ten per cent. That is so also with respect to West Indian commodities provided for by the treaty and the Customs Act. But the difficulty was that in the case mentioned by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) the rice did not qualify with respect to either under the statutory conditions and therefore was subject to the higher impost. I felt, and I think I did indicate to the minister at that time, that the ruling should be changed, but it was indicated to me,-and I am bound to say it seemed to me to be fairly so-that if you make an exception in favour of direct importation into Canada from the country of origin, you never know where you will end, and that it is better to stick to the principle rather than depart from it. That is what the government of that day did. I am bound to say I thought the reason given me at the time was sound and I did not raise the matter in the house, for reasons that the hon. member can understand-that if I suggested an exception to the rule, and he suggested an exception to the rule, and some one else suggested an exception to the rale, then the rule with respect to direct shipment vanishes and the benefit disappears.
I think it is just a question of the wisdom of the rule.

This is a
substantial increase of twenty-five cents on the general and the intermediate. I suppose the usual pledge is given that the price will not be increased, but our experience in this particular commodity is that cleaned rice has brought the same price plus the duty paid.

In the United States
they charge two and a half cents a pound. In this country that has not been the case. Last year our production amounted to $1,400,000.

the duty. If that were not so, then what in the name of common sense is the use of increasing these duties so much? The question answers itself.

speechtext: There is one in Vancouver and one in Montreal of which I know; those two come to my mind at the moment.

But is it not a fact, Mr. Chairman, that this industry is not entirely in the hands of Canadians in Vancouver, and that this does not really help Canadians? My information is that the majority of workers are Chinese or Japanese who are not citizens of this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend has raised a question which is far removed from tariff discussion. I could not answer the question, but at least this is a Canadian industry. The question of employment is a matter with which the provincial authorities have power to deal. I can only indicate that this would not be so with respect to the Montreal plant, so far as I know, and it does follow that in a good many industries to which the hon. gentleman might refer there are employed men and women who have come from other parts of the world. In some cases they are naturalized and in others they are not, but in the main they are naturalized Canadians and I do not think the fact that their employers avail themselves of the services of some employees who may not be Canadians should militate against the soundness of the principle that if possible this industry should be allowed to supply the requirements of the Canadian people, provided the tariff is not used for the purpose of exploitation.

I wanted to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to the Canada Year Book, in dealing with this question of rice. I notice that there are six rice mills in Canada, having twenty-seven salaried employees who were paid $74,000 and fifty-one wage earners, who were paid $52,000. According to the government reports, for the year ending March 31, 1930, we imported 175,884 hundredweight of cleaned rice and 402,923 hundredweight of uncleaned rice; the cost of the cleaned rice was about $3.92 a hundredweight, while the cost of the uncleaned rice was $2.99 per hundredweight, leaving a difference of almost $1 per hundredweight which would be available for cleaning purposes. Having that in mind I wonder whether there can be any necessity for increasing the duty on rice to $1 a hundredweight which, if these figures are correct, would give the rice mills $2 per hundredweight for cleaning a commodity which is worth about 3 cents a pound.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is worth nearly 4 cents a pound on invoices of importations, and the raw rice is worth nearly 3 cents per pound at invoice prices. To that must be added transportation costs, including insurance, freight and brokerage charges. The result has been what I have indicated, that at present rates the industry has been threatened by importations from other parts of the world. If there is no increase in price-and if there is an increase the benefits that may accrue from this duty will be removed-it is believed that the maintenance of that source of supply in Canada for Canadians is beneficial to this country.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

In regard to the duty on hay, the finance minister admits that the imports of hay are insignificant compared with the exports. The imposition of this $5 duty simply means that that amount will be added to the price which the consumer of hay pays, and many importers of hay are actual farmers. I have no doubt that hay is sold in certain sections of Alberta and British Columbia to mining men and to lumber men, but it is also true that it is sold to farmers, and since the average price paid for imported hay is $15.54, it simply means that this $5 duty will be added to the price which these consumers of hay have to pay. It simply means

that other industries will have to pay the duty. It is another illustration of how continually rising prices are going to raise production costs all around.

Cannot the farmers grow
their own hay?
The house should remember that this is an item that does not in any degree, or at least only to a very slight degree, affect the farmers of Quebec and Ontario.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, northern Ontario.

It may affect northern
Ontario to a very limited extent. In Ontario the only importation of hay is by way of the Soo, I presume.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the Soo.

I tried to find out at just
what point it entered Canada, and I was not able to get the information. While hay may be bought in northern Ontario by other than farmers, frequently it is bought by the farmers themselves. It will simply have the effect of raising the price of hay by $5 a ton. To show you the difference between imports and exports, and how little this means to the farmers of Canada as a whole, I will give the figures for just one year. In 1926 we exported 368,787 tons of hay, valued at $3,711,840, and we imported in the same year 8,510 tons, valued at $142,249. I have the figures for five years, but it is not necessary to give them, because the figures for 1926 illustrate the situation as it is. Probably it will be heralded all over the Dominion that the government is taking great care of the farmers by putting this duty on hay, but to the vast majority of the farmers of Canada it means nothing at all.

I should like to ask
my hon. friend what is the present price of hay in Lisgar?

I am afraid that if the
present crop conditions continue hay may go to $40 or $50 a ton in Lisgar.

This is another case, Mr
Chairman, where the poultryman in British Columbia is going to be made the victim. Not content with thrusting the sword into his vitals by putting a duty on corn, the weapon is now to be turned in the wound by increasing the price of another product that he buys largely, and must buy, and that is alfalfa hay. He cannot raise it on his scanty five acres, because it is not adapted to the growing of alfalfa. Only comparatively small areas of British Columbia are adapted to the growing of alfalfa. But the poultryman must have alfalfa hay, and of a particular grade. If I remember correctly, it is the second or third cutting that he requires, the first cutting being too rank [DOT] and coarse, and not having the proper foliage. He obtains from the western states the alfalfa that he needs for feed. This duty may possibly, as the hon. member for Lisgar says, benefit a few hay producers in the southern part, presumably, of the interior of British Columbia. I would like, however, to point out to the house this fact, which is perhaps not generally known; it is very bad economics to encourage the farmer to sell hay, because when he does that he is selling his farm piecemeal. It has been calculated by government experts that when you sell a ton of timothy hay-and the loss would be greater in the case of alfalfa- whatever price you get for it you have depreciated the value of your land by ten or eleven dollars, because you have taken practically all the fertilizer value away and left nothing there in return. You have depreciated your farm. The expression is common among farmers that such and such a man will not get ahead because he is selling his farm piecemeal. There is nothing to replace the fertility that has been taken out of the soil if the farmer sells his hay. It is calculated -this is not my opinion; if you go to the Minister of Agriculture he will tell you the same thing-that the loss to a farm in fertilizer content by selling a ton of butter is somewhere in the neighbourhood of only 50 cents, and it takes a good many tons of hay to produce a ton of butter. That illustrates how short-sighted is the farmer who persistently sells off his hay. His farm cannot long endure it. It is bad farm economics to pursue. It is a well known fact that the man who buys feed buys fertilizer, and oil cake meal or other such feeds and brings them onto his farm increases its value. As the saying goes: More fertilizer more grass, more grass more cattle, more cattle more fertilizer, in an ever enlarging circle of prosperity. Those are matters however which
effect the hay producer; they are his troubles, not mine. The proposed duty will add S3 a ton to the cost of one of the items of the poultryman's expenditure and will accrue to the benefit of some producer who has devoted his energies to the selling of hay.

The increase in the duty on hay is to the extent of 250 per cent. In the year 1930 we imported 4,502 tons of hay valued at $61,175, or at a rate of about $15 a ton. All of that hay came from the United States or from Alaska. During the same period we exported 162,000 tons valued at $2,007,944. Of that tonnage 35,179 tons went to the United States, valued at $321,000, or an average price of a little less than $9 a ton. From these figures hon. members will see that while our imports were valued at $15 a ton, our exports were valued at only $9 a ton. Why the difference? The explanation is that hay is not a commodity which will stand shipment across a continent; it is too bulky, and the freight rate is too high. If a part of Canada is suffering from a hay famine it will look for its supply to the nearest point from which that supply can be obtained, and purchases are frequently made in the United States. It is much cheaper to bring that hay in from the United States than to bring it across the continent and pay higher freight rates. That accounts for the fact that our imports are valued at a much higher rate than our exports. The few thousand tons we import are brought into different parts of Canada where there is no supply or where there may be a hay famine. I have said that while we buy only 4,502 tons from the United States we sell to them 35,179 tons. Are we going to jeopardize our market for 35,000 tons, in round figures, in order to shut out the 4,500 tons which we must have and which our own growers in other parts of Canada because of freight rates are not in a position to supply? Will the minister not learn anything from what happened in New Zealand? Will he not learn anything about what happened to his potatoes? Will he not learn about what is likely to happen in the Argentine when he shuts out their corn? Does he not think the United States will retaliate and shut out our 35,000 tons of hay because we are attempting to exclude their 4,500 tons?
What is the duty on Canadian hay going into the United States?

I do not know. I have not the rate before me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Many orders in council have been promulgated. They appear in the Canada Gazette. It is not to be expected that I can carry in my head all the orders n council that have been promulgated, and knowing the hon. gentleman's industry, I am sure that, by perusal of the Gazette from Saturday to Saturday, he knows just as much about the matter as anyone else.

The difficulty is that they last only four days sometimes. One must be agile to follow the changes made by order in council fixing values. My right hon. friend apparently had suddenly brought to his attention the fact that a serious mistake had been made in the fixing of values on potatoes; because I notice that in four days' time-perhaps it was a little longer-the change was made from potatoes to radishes. I never was able to understand why that action was taken so suddenly by the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no doubt that necessary changes may be made in a single day; at least I hope so.
From potatoes to radishes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No; that would not be quite sufficient for the hon. gentleman. It was not changed from potatoes to radishes. There is scarcely an hon. member who is not familiar with the fact that goods that were to be exported from Canada to the United States at a time when a bargain was made were subject to a higher duty before they reached there. In many instances, where it is found that a situation has suddenly developed threatening the life of a Canadian industry, whether it be potatoes or radishes or anything else, action will be taken as quickly as possible. And in the case of potatoes action was taken with respect to what I might call old potatoes-that is, the carry-over which the farmeT was anxious to get rid of before the new season began. The statute was not intended to cover that particular class of potato. The order was put into operation and remained in operation until it had served the purpose intended1. Radishes had nothing to do with that; it was an entirely different transaction. When potatoes were taken out of the item, radishes remained. There are other commodities to which I need hardly refer-cherries, strawberries, lettuce, asparagus, apricots, raspberries, peas, beets, cabbage, carrots, cauliflower, celery, cucumbers, and eo on. With respect to these articles, I put this question to my hon. friends opposite who are agriculturists: Whether we should not have what I may call immediate tariff action to save the situation. The season in some countries is much more forward this year than last year, and the seasonal tariff must therefore vary with the season in the community affected. When our vegetables and fruits are ripe, it follows that south o'f us they have ripened previously; and if the foreign vegetables and fruits come into this country they will, unless some action is taken, displace our fruits and vegetables. The reason is a simple one. The season is ending in one country just as it begins in the other, and the surplus, the accumulated product which is left over after having satisfied the requirements of the country in which it is grown, is available for export to Canada. Now, unless we are able to take immediate action to prevent it, the effort and labour of our fruit growers and vegetable growers will be destroyed. Whenever it is necessary, therefore, proper action has been taken. And such action will continue to be taken. If we are wrong we shall be replaced by others who will do what is

But so far as this government is concerned, it proposes to proceed1 on that principle and to endeavour, by the use of this instrument, which is the only one I know of adequate for the purpose, to secure to the Canadian vegetable and fruit grower an equal opportunity to compete with the producers of other countries. It gets back to that fundamental principle. It is the privilege of the house to censure the administration for taking such action, but I have no hesitation in saying that this is the principle upon which we shall proceed so long as we are here.

On section 1.-Requirements for certificates of service as masters and mates.
What is the purpose of this bill?

Under the Canada Shipping Act a master without a certificate may sail a fishing vessel, but he may not sail a vessel that ceases to be a fishing vessel. Owing to the economic depression, which has affected the shipping industry in eastern Canada as it has, for instance, wheat growing in the west, a large number of vesels are not now fishing and are engaged in other lines. The masters cannot sail them although many of them own a substantial share in the vessels. The result has been that a great number of vessels of Canadian registry have been transferred to the registry of Newfoundland or Barbados, which do not require certificated masters. The purpose of this bill, which introduces no new principle-the principle was adopted in 1920-is to enable a man who de facto has had experience within any one of ten years previous to 1931 to go before the examining board and take certain examinations which are specified in the explanatory notes to the bill-as to his sobriety, experience, ability and general good conduct on board ship, and a sight test-and upon passing those tests he gets his certificate. The principle was adopted, as I say, in 1920.

Mr. Speaker, the bill consists of two distinct clauses which seek to. do away with certain anomalies in the present Immigration Act. In the last few years there have been a very iarge number of deportations from Canada. Last year 1,806 were deported as public charges; 701 because of convictions for criminal offences, and inmates of penitentiaries and gaoils; 71 on account of convictions under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act; 445 inmates of mental institutions, including insane persons, feeble minded persons, epileptics and mental defectives; 320 physical defectives; 97 because of misrepresentations and stealth; 5 on account of having been previously deported; 70 miscellaneous cases, and 510 dependent members of families accompanying deports.
I recognize quite clearly that it is very difficult to have passed by this house any public bill introduced by a private member. As a matter of fact in the last five years only three public bills introduced by private members have actually passed the house. Therefore I am under no illusions as to the possibility of my bill becoming law. I can quite readily understand that there are other sections of the Immigration Act which should be modified. I realize further that the proposals I am making may not be the very wisest conceivable, and that the department may see fit to bring forward others. I bring two matters to the attention of the house, however, in connection with what I believe to be certain hardships existing under the act. If the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) can find any better way of meeting the needs I have outlined I shall be very glad to accept his suggestions.
Immigration Act

The first clause in my amendment reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act or any amendment thereof or regulations made thereunder, an immigrant who has completed ten years continuous residence in Canada, shall not thereafter be liable to deportation.
A large number of people have come to Canada in good faith, have lived here probably ten, fifteen or eighteen years and yet have had no opportunity to establish domicile or permanent residence. For that reason they are liable to deportation. It seems to me some limitation should be placed upon the period during which deportation proceedings may be taken. A year ago our attention was called to a number of cases concerning epileptic women who had been placed in institutions and at the request of the provincial authorities, who found their care a burden, were deported. Surely anybody who has been in Canada for fifteen years has acquired some rights. If before that period of time has elapsed the authorities have not discovered something wrong with them and deported them I think they ought to be allowed to remain, and we ought to accept the responsibility. In a ten-year period undoubtedly they will have severed their connections with the old country; the likelihood is that their families will have been broken up and they will have no home to return to should they be deported. Under the circumstances I think it but reasonable that we should place some limitation upon the time within which such deportations may be carried out, and I have suggested ten years as a reasonable period.
The second clause of the bill is of a different character. It attempts to recognize a right of citizenship on the part of persons who in good faith have come to this country and lived here for a number of years, but for some reason or another have been forced for the time being to go to the United States or elsewhere on this continent to seek employment. I do not suppose that from this time forward there will be so many of that class, because the people of the United States have put up the bars against immigration and it is not easy for people living in Canada to get to the other side of the line. In the past, however, a great many people have come to Canada, especially to the western country, intending to make it their home. There came a time when they were unable to find work; some of them were induced to go to Chicago. Detroit or other larger centres of the United States to seek employment. After a while their employment ceased and they desired to return to Canada, but were refused readmission. Apparently they had forfeited all

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
subtopic: DEPORTATION-RIGHT TO RETURN TO CANADA AFTER ABSENCE
speechtext:
With respect to
this bill I must compliment the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) upon the moderation with which he expressed his views in connection with a subject which in large measure, has to do with the human equation. I am not unmindful of the interest the hon. member takes in questions of this character.
I am opposed to the bill. Section 3 of the Immigration Act is the one which would be affected if this bill became law, since that is the section which has to do with prohibited classes. With Tpsnect to prohibited classes
some criticism has been offered in the recent past, and in fact for very many years past. In dealing with immigration we must bear in mind that heretofore the Dominion government has directed, encouraged and controlled -and I use the word "controlled" with a degree of hesitancy-migration into Canada. What responsibilities does that immediately create? If care is not taken in the encouragement of peoples to come to this country, and if no discipline is exercised, upon whom falls the responsibility? Once an immigrant is legally landed in Canada undoubtedly he acquires a certain status under our laws. He has a perfect right to go from one province to another, or from one city or town to another, and the responsibility for that person is cast upon the province or the municipality in which he happens to be. Therefore I suggest that parliament in a matter of this kind should exercise extreme care, though not by any means to the point of exclusion. While at present there must be a degree of rigidity which in normal times would not be exercised, yet at all times great care should be exercised, and particularly at a time like this, although under normal conditions desirable people undoubtedly would be welcomed in this country. Upon whom falls the burden? In a period of depression these matters come into bold relief, let me say.
During the two years prior to last summer new peoples came to Canada to the extent of almost a quarter of a million, including almost 100,000 adult males. Where are those people to-day? They either displaced Canadian labour or they themselves are to-day in the ranks of the unemployed. That is the situation that faces the people of this country. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is, I believe, and always has been an ardent advocate of the labouring man. I myself, while probably not as well known as he in my advocacy, am considered, I believe, in those restricted areas where I am known, as having been not unmindful of the labouring man's needs.
The introduction of new people into this country in large numbers, at a time when thoughtful Canadians must have known that we were approaching and were then, indeed, actually in a period of depression, was a direct challenge to the worker in Canada. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, in his sincere advocacy of labour, must recognize that, I am sure. When this department was given to me to administer that was one of the first things I had to take into consideration, and it was not a time when one could allow one's sympathies to be unduly the guide. I have great sympathv for any human being
Immigration Act

who is having a hard struggle to get along. I have great sympathy for those new people who came into the country in years gone by and even for those who came in the near past, and it is no source of satisfaction to me to see them now in the ranks of the unemployed. But when it comes to changing the law of the country in the way proposed in this bill, I tell the house that my sympathy first goes to the worker of Canada, who needs the protection of a law such as our Immigration Act. And while in the administration of that act I may make mistakes, they will certainly be made in favour of the working men of Canada as against people from other countries, because those other countries have responsibilities of their own with regard to their own nationals.
Unquestionably one's sympathy often goes out to those who have to be deported. But let me point out that if this act became law and the officials of the Immigration department were divested of the authority to send back to their country of origin those people who do not comply with our law, then I should be obliged at this time to allow into Canada tens of thousands of people who are in a situation similar to that referred to by the hon. member. Of course those people would come into Canada, because the United States are determined to send them back to their country of origin. They would come to the border and declare that they had lived in Canada at one time and wished to come back. Why? Because, if they did not get the chance to come in, they would be sent back to their country of origin. They would not be allowed to remain in the United States, either because they do not comply with the laws of that country or because their presence in that country is not desired.
Now, can we in the interests of the labouring man of Canada take such steps as this bill would seem to contemplate? In view of the dispassionate way in which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has discussed the bill, I suggest that we can afford to take no such step as this bill proposes. From time to time, under the present law, deportations have to be made. The provinces and the municipalities have rights. In the poorer municipalities of northern Canada the burden of taking care of people who are not able to take care of themselves, by reason of physical and mental defects, is thrust upon the public. And those municipalities are having a hard enough struggle as it is to get along, without having that additional burden thrown upon them.

speechtext: Does not the minister think that the officials responsible at the gates should, in the first instance, keep out such people, or Should discover within the first ten years that they are undesirable?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
subtopic: DEPORTATION-RIGHT TO RETURN TO CANADA AFTER ABSENCE
speechtext:
That question has been
asked me many times. Many cases have passed our immigration officials, and I doubt seriously whether the officials could possibly have discovered defects that existed without introducing a system of inspection that would be most irritating to many people who would pass with a very casual inspection. It is true, the time seems long; and it might be said with some degree of force that the defects should be detected. But it is utterly impossible for the Department of Immigration to employ a sufficient number of officials to follow up all immigrants coming into Canada to find out whether or not they entered legally. The onus is surely upon the immigrant seeking entry into Canada to see that he complies with the laws of the country, and not upon the Dominion to supply a preventive or investigating force to follow up each immigrant year after year to see whether or not on his arrival he complied with the law.
In cases of deportation every chance of appeal is given. Boards of inquiry are established and appeals are available. Evidence is taken. Nothing is done in a haphazard way, and while occasionally hardship ensues, yet if we founded our general law upon any provision to meet one or two cases of hardship, then we should be adopting a most dangerous principle; for a great number of people who come in legally would be immediately affected by the introduction of that general law made to apply to a particular case. That would not be at all desirable.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre spoke about the desirability of recognizing that a person coming to Canada should have the right freely to go over to the United States and return, crossing and recrossing the boundary as fancy suited him, in his search for employment. The hon. member suggested that a man W'ho out of a job should have that right to cross and recross the boundary. That is not my conception of what should be done in that regard.

speechtext:
The minister asked me to give him a concrete case. This man Michael Corahe, a Pole, was ordered deported by the United States immigration authorities. He had served four years in the Canadian army. He came to Canada at the age of five and enlisted at sixteen. Eight years ago he went to the United States. He was unable

Immigration Act
to reenter Canada. He was a naturalized Canadian, his brother and sisters were bom in Canada and are now in Toronto. It would seem to me that that is a case of real hardship.

I have the record of that case. This man was allowed entry into Canada, but I may say that it was with reluctance I permitted his entry. He was born in Poland and came to Canada in 1907 with his parents. He was in the Canadian forestry corps between May, 1917, and July, 1919, being discharged at Winnipeg. He applied for admission to Canada from the United States in October, 1930, claiming to have resided in this country from 1907 to May, 1930, having proceeded to the United States to reside on the latter date. He was rejected, being unable to comply with the occupational and passport requirements of the law. The department, in view of previous residence, further investigated the case and it was ascertained that this man had not proceeded to the United States in 1930 but had been working in Detroit for approximately eight years. Despite the misrepresentation and the length of residence out of Canada, the department allowed entry in view of previous residence in this country from childhood and because of the man's military service. The hon member will see that his instructions in this case do not coincide with the facts. I reluctantly gave an order allowing this man to return to Canada.
Criticisms will be levelled from time to time at the Department of Immigration, but I propose to assume full responsibility, both for the policies of the department and the acts of its officials. At times I will make mistakes, and then I will have to rely upon the generosity of those who criticize. The rule in the department is to see that the laws of the country are observed. Every departure therefrom is a step forward in imperilling the position of the Canadian worker, whose cause is so strongly advocated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I believe if the hon. member thinks this matter over he will agree that w'hile there may be some merit in his bill, if it should pass it would be an added hardship to the man who has come to this country, established his home and is bringing up a family. The jobs of workers in this country would be imperilled by permitting any indiscriminate crossing between the United States and
Canada, as times are better here or better there. I believe that the worker who has established his home and family in this country should get every bit of protection which our law allows and should be given preference against the transient worker who is ready to go wherever fields look the greenest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I agree almost
entirely with what the hon. minister has just said, that those who have established homes in and are residents of Canada should receive consideration, I should like to draw to his attention a case which I took up with the department before he assumed charge of it, which has caused me to feel that I should support this bill. This was a British subject, born in the old land, who came to Canada and had resided here for some twelve or thirteen years. He homesteaded just a few miles from me, and while pursuing his occupation as a farmer he met with an accident which brought about complications which, in his opinion, could not be successfully dealt with by the doctors in Canada. He went to the United States to some place where he was advised he could obtain treatment, but probably neglected to tell the authorities that he would be gone for more than six months. He stayed in the United States for eighteen months, and when he found that the treatment was not giving the results he expected he attempted to return to his home. He was stopped by the immigration authorities, who claimed that he was not a Canadian citizen. He had nothing to show that he was a Canadian citizen, although he was a British subject. I was wired about this young man, and I took the matter up wTith the then Minister of Immigration. I was told that if the United States was determined to deport him there was only one place to which they could deport him, and that was back to Scotland. Although this man had had twelve or thirteen years' residence in Canada, the authorities claimed that he had no domicile here. It is because of this case that I feel I must support the bill. It may be, as the minister has said, that the door will be opened wider, but I do not think it is fair to the minister or to the department to ask them to give special consideration to any one immigrant. For these reasons, I assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that I have a great deal of sympathy with his bill.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Was that man deported?
Supply-Geological Survey

M,r. VALLANCE: No, he was not. However, it was not the law that prevented that deportation, it was simply the courtesy of the department in allowing him to reenter Canada.
