Mr. LaVERGNE : May I inquire from the minister whether the British Empire Settlement Act is still in force, and what the scope of that act is so far as immigration to Canada is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The British Empire Settlement Act, of course, is an act of the imperial parliament. Generally it provides for assistance in the movement of British peoples to the various dominions. I think we are not alone just now so far as the dominions are concerned with respect to restrictions under the agreement.
Mr. LaVERGNE : I understand that under that act a certain amount is loaned to the sett'ler-immigrant coming to Canada to tide him over his first years, and that he reimburses the money to the government when he has made enough .money to do so. I think, and I believe this was understood by the convention at AVinnipeg, that first aid should be given to the Canadian, and that the best way to settle our country is to settle it with our own people. We should profit by the mistake of the United States. It is years ago since I raised my voice in the house on this subject. I have not changed my opinion since then. I still believe that it is not by filling our country with foreigners that we are going to build it up. It should be filled up according to the traditions of the country. More important than material prosperity is moral and intellectual prosperity. I am not allowed to refer to a past debate, but only to-night we had an instance of what happens: some people who come heTe do not think enough of this coun-

Supply-Immigration
try to become naturalized Canadians. They run about with their troubles and sometimes their diseases, physical, moral or intellectual. I do not know whether the British Empire settlement policy is still in force, but if we can afford to lend money to immigrants from other countries to settle here, we can very well afford to do it for our own people. I understand that to-day it costs less for a man to leave Liverpool and settle in the west than it does for a settler from the province of Quebec, the lower provinces or the province of Ontario. My opinion is that the best immigrant to fill up the west is the Canadian immigrant from the old provinces, who is already assimilated, who knows the traditions which the Englishspeaking and French-speaking Canadians have cherished in this country for the last one hundred and fifty j'ears.

Might I point out that vote No. 125 deals specifically with what my hon. friend is now discussing?
Mr. LaVERGNE: I am very glad the hon. gentleman called me to order. I do not want to take up the time of the committee when I am not on the right item, but when that other item is reached, I shall have an opportunity to speak. I repeat that the best migration with which to settle Canada is Canadian migration, and if any favours are to be given they should be given to Canadians. It is very unfortunate that .people should come here from foreign countries and receive special favours when Canadians cannot settle in another part of the country which so long has been theirs.

We have been told that for the past few months immigration to this country has practically ceased, yet we find that while there was $324,000 spent last year, $312,000 is to be spent this year. Hon. members will notice that there is but a slight reduction, and I am wondering why the staff is being kept in service.
Mr. LaVERGNE: To keep them out.

Nobody is being allowed to come in, yet we have this large amount being paid in salaries.
Mr. LaVERGNE: To keep them out.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
In answer to the hon.
member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) may I say that I am thoroughly in accord with much that he has said. I assure him that no assistance such as he has suggested has been given by this government to people from other lands. In connection with the British migrants to Canada I trust-and I believe that the hon.
member for Montmagny will agree with me- that the time will never come when the Britisher will not be welcomed in Canada. I think my hon. friend will join with me in welcoming all Britishers who have come to Canada "under their own steam" and are prepared to take care of themselves. That is the position to-day. We are not advancing moneys nor have we advanced moneys with the exception of certain cases where assisted passages have been given. Outside of existing agreements which will shortly expire that practice has been entirely discontinued.
Replying to the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly), I have found it much more difficult to keep people out of Canada than to bring them in. Even during this period of depression, strange to say, there are many people striving to get in. In fact if the effort to come into Canada is any indication of our recovery from the depression I should say that we are recovering very rapidly, because we require a large staff along our boundary lines to see that those who should not be allowed into Canada are with the least possible irritation kept out. I should like to indicate to my hon. friend the importance of the work that these men are doing. The records of the Immigration Department disclose that during the last calendar year the officers along our boundary line passed into Canada, either for temporary visits of only an hour or two or for longer periods, excluding immigrants and entries at ocean ports, over 32,000,000 people. Hon members will readily recognize the necessity for a well organized and disciplined preventive force.

In how many j'ears did
that number enter Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In one year. In the month of August alone the number was over 6,000,000.

I agree with the remarks of my hon. friend from Montmagny, and it is rather interesting that at the present time everj'body seems to be endeavouring to discourage immigration. That, however, has not always been so, and the government of which I had the honour to be a member was strongly assailed because it was not taking steps to increase the population of Canada and to bring in immigrants. That criticism was made as recently as the 1929 session. I shall quote from Hansard of 1929, page 22, where the present Prime Minister is reported as follows:
Is there any Canadian who regards this problem as being adequately dealt with by the present system? We have here one of the largest undeveloped areas in the world; we have a very pressing necessity for more people. There need be no misapprehension about that, notwithstanding what has been said from tima
Supply-Immigration

to time to the contrary. It will be found that the increase of population in this country, brought about through bringing additional people in, will not only lessen unemployment for those who are now in it, but will increase all employment. Those who have studied the problems connected with the movement of people realize that instead of there being a diminution of opportunities for labour, the now of new peoples into a country means the increasing of the opportunities for those who are there as well as providing work to those who may come.
In view of certain statements which have been made, more particularly in my province, I wish to remind the committee that we were attacked not because we were bringing too many immigrants but because we were not bringing enough.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	I am glad to see that
the memory of my hon. friend goes back at least two or three years. Probably due to the fact that I am getting old mine goes back much farther than that. I can remember in the good old days back in 1905 and 1906, when immigrants were coming to Canada at the rate of about 500,000 a year. I remember the time when I was assailed in this house because I thought that the ratio of immigrants to population was far too high. That was in the old days of the North Atlantic Trading Company and the Saskatchewan Land Settlement Company.

Who was in that deal?
Mr. LaVERGNE : I remember giving figures at a time when the population of the United States was about 52,000,000 and ours was about 7,000,000 or 8,000,000. We were begging for immigrants to come here, with the result that we filled up our country and to-day we are beginning to pay the piper. The theories which have certain currency out west, especially in the city of Winnipeg, were practically ignored in Canada at that time. When we imported those immigrants we imported their doctrines of very advanced socialism, and probably communism. We introduced into our country the famous Doukhobors and many others which have not greatly improved our population. I agree with the Minister of Immigration that we should build up our country with the two basic races, those of British and French descent, which are already assimilated. I hope my hon. friend's memory will go back 'to a time about twenty-five years ago, as it did to the resolution he read a minute ago, when I was laughed at in the house because I made the statement that we

were sacrificing the intellectual and moral prosperity of our country for material prosperity Which would prove in the future to be dangerous to Canada.

Two years ago my hon. friend would not have agreed with this program, either.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Certainly not. I am
open to conviction, but until it is proved I am wrong I hold to my view. I think if my hon. friends went to the United States and talked with any patriotic American who belonged to the good old Yankee stock or belonged to the southerners-

One hundred per cent
American.
Mr. LaVERGNE: I would interject at this point that the 100 per cent American of fifty years ago has practically disappeared. I should think that the smell of the melting pot in the United States should open our eyes and caution us to go slowly when we are filling up our country, and impress us with the necessity for building our citizenship with the Canadian races which are already assimilated. We know of the common traditions in Canada which are absorbed by the British and French people who should constitute our population. Let us fill up our country with the sons of the soil, the sons of people who are inspired by the traditions of 150 year's of common life with our English-speaking compatriots. This is the beat immigration. Why this hurry in filling up our country with all the riff-raff of Europe? In this way are we going to make Canada happier and more prosperous? I think Canada, especially the province of Quebec, is prosperous in a way that other nations may well envy. I do not think any people in the world enjoy more happiness and more liberty, and have a greater respect for the rights of others than the people of the province of Quebec. And that enviable condition is due to the traditions which have been handed down to us by our forefathers for the past 300 years. I think the democracy that has been built up in that province is an outstanding example to the world in freedom, in happiness, in contentment, and in respect for the rights of others, especially of minorities.

I had intended to deal
with this question on votes 124 and 125, but inasmuch as it has been discussed on this particular item I suppose I may as well continue it. I was very happy to hear what I considered the very courageous remarks of the hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gor-

Supply-Immigration
don) with respect to immigration, especially when he said he was not going to permit the dictation of railroad companies or of immigration agents to continue any longer. The only trouble I see is that he will not only have to offset their dictation, he will have also to offset their influence. I have had some experience in this regard, before I entered t'he cabinet, while I was a member of the cabinet and since I have tried to maintain the position that he is trying to maintain at the present time. If I failed in that regard it was because of the political manoeuvring of hon. friends opposite who now support the government.
I noticed in the Ottawa Journal of March 22, 1930, a despatch stating that the agent of one particular church wishes to double the number of our British settlers. I may say to the minister that the Catholic church, the United church and the Salvation Army are striving to bring in settlers. They have men engaged in that work, and those men seem to think that the greater the number of settlers they can induce to come to this country the more important their respective positions will become. In 1931, an official of the Salvation Army, Lieut.-Commissioner W. J. Barnard Turner, of London, England, visited this country and stated that he was seeking to move 2,000,000 Britishers to Canada. I see that votes 124 and 125 oover grants to assist that gentleman to carry out his plan.

Mr'. HEENAN: I am heart and soul with the minister in his endeavour to stop immigration, but I do not think for a moment that he is doing so. The minister admits that Britishers are permitted to enter who oome "under their own steam" as he says.
Why should Britishers or any other nationals be allowed to come into this country "under their own steam" and flood the labour market?
I do not think we should allow Britishers to come in freely, especially when we know they are encouraged by the propaganda of immigration societies to come to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
What propaganda does
my hon. friend refer to?

At the present time their agents are travelling throughout the British isles telling the people what fine prospects there are in Canada for intending immigrants. In my room only yesterday a young returned soldier from the British isles-from the same part of the country as I came from-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I hope we did not deport him.

No, they are all decent people who come from that part of the country. He asked me to get him a job and I am trying to do so. I inquired why he came to this country. He told me that throughout Britain to-day there are immigration officers paid by the different churches and citizen's committees urging young men to come to this country, and offering to lend them money to pay their passage. Those agents are telling the people that immigration into Canada from continental Europe being practically stopped, now is the time for them to come in as a preferred class so that when conditions improve they will be right on the job.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: What churches?
All the churches; I am not speaking of any particular church.
Nonsense.
There is no one in the house better acquainted with what is nonsense than the hon. member who has just interrupted me.
Where do you stand on this question?
I do not want to be further interrupted. When I was Minister of Labour I was obstructed by gentlemen of his calibre who did not know the difference between common sense and nonsense.

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. MacDonald, South Cape Breton):
speechtext: Do not invite reprisals, please.

There are citizen's committees going up and down the British isles, especially in the industrial centres in the north of England. The members of those com-
Supply-Immigration

mittees make house to house calls asking the boys to emigrate as a matter of patriotism. This is the formula: You joined the colours at a certain time in 1914; it is just as necessary to join our band now and emigrate to Canada, Australia and other parts of the British empire in order to save the situation in England. There is an impression throughout the country that the government has stopped immigration and yet the minister tells the house that anyone who comes here "under his own steam" is received with open arms. I hope the minister will be successful in stopping political propaganda and overcoming political influence, because if there is anything that will tend to destroy Canada as a country for immigrants it will be political manoeuvring.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Might I ask just what the hon. member means by political manoeuvring?

I will give it to you in a few moments, and when I get through you will not have any doubt of what I mean. In 1915 the Conservative government of Ontario thought it wise to appoint a royal commission on unemployment. The report of that commission was delivered in 1916, and from that time to the present propaganda has been circulated to induce people to come to this country from all parts of the world. I find the following at page 50 of the report of the royal commission appointed by the Ontario government:
_ Your commission recommends such reform in immigration methods as will make directly for the settlement of Canada's vacant agricultural areas, stimulate the development of the country's natural resources and combat the universal tendency of population to concentrate in cities. Your commissioners would further advise such united action by the imperial and dominion authorities as will lead a greater proportion of British immigrants to the overseas dominions instead of to foreign countries, thus conserving the man power, and adding to the strength and wealth of the empire. For these economic and patriotic reasons the dose of the war should find us ready with a courageous inter-imperial immigration policy in which the imperial, dominion and provincial governments and railway and other great employing corporations will have a responsible share. For Canada the primary problem is to bring the right sort of people to the land and to assist them in every way possible to make the land productive and themselves prosperous citizens of the dominion. If necessary, the governments interested should furnish such financial assistance as will enable the newcomers within a reasonable time to become self-supporting on the soil.
Carrying on from that point, we find the politicians interesting themselves in immigration, and during the last dominion election we had Mr. Ferguson saying too many people were coming to this country. I caught him 
deliberately .misrepresenting facts, as is well known; he spoke of a protest he had made to Ottawa, meaning of course to the Dominion government, but finally he had to confess that he had protested to Sir William Clark, High Commissioner for Great Britain in Canada. I find the following editorial comment in the Brockville Recorder and Times of December 1, 1928:
Mr. Ferguson addresses the transportation club in Toronto and says, in part, that:
"In the first place, we cannot hope to populate this country with British people alone. There are only a few millions to spare at most, and when we talk about bringing people and putting them on the land one has only to learn that in the British Isles there are only three million farmers, to understand there is not much of a source to draw from in that respect. But there are large areas of the continent from which we can draw most desirable people, who have characteristics so much like our own, and who can be readily assimilated into our Canadian life and make good Canadian citizens and good British subjects."
Those were Mr. Ferguson's words, two years before the election.
My hon. friend quotes from the Brockville Recorder and Times. I should like to ask who is the owner, proprietor and general manager of the Brockville Recorder and Times.

I do not know. I do not know who owns or controls any paper in Canada, and I am not very much interested. But I can tell the hon. gentleman, who is a good friend of .mine, that these; are the words uttered by Mr. Ferguson; they are not the words of the editor of the newspaper.
When and where was Mr. Ferguson supposed to have made that statement?

I;f the hon. gentleman will just follow me I will give him all that Howard Ferguson ever said, and that is not much. In 1930 Mr. Ferguson said we were bringing too many immigrants to this country, but I quote his words from the Toronto Star of October 5, 1928:
"There are splendid migrants in Britain," he said, "anxious and willing to come to the new portion of the empire. Some of them have cauliflower ears and hare lips; some have flat feet. But we have lots of fellows of that kind in this country and they get along splendidly. But as long as we take the position that there will be no more hare lips than what we produce ourselves, of course we are going to discourage immigration."
He wanted people with hare lips and bow legs and everything else.

What do you mean by that?

Supply-Immigration

I continue quoting:
"Let us be sensible about it. If it was not necessary when we brought out those harvesters to ask more than three or four questions, and tell them if they found jobs they could stay here, why ask four or five sheets of family history and set up technical difficulties for others? There are a lot of little, irritating things that can easily be removed, and I am quite sure, having had it brought to their notice, the government at Ottawa will see that they are removed."
Premier Ferguson intimated that if it lay in his power he would encourage any movement to Canada from Sweden.
"What they need in Norway," he continued, "and what all Europe needs, and what the British Isles need, is more accurate, truthful stories about the conditions that exist in this country, if we are to get immigration. In every country I was in I visited-
He had just returned -from a trip to Europe.
In every country I was in I visited some of the transportation offices. In some, I visited a great number, and everywhere I asked for literature about Ontario. I found some agents had never heard of such a place, and where I did get literature it was Canadian literature-
You see, he does not think Canadian literature is worth much unless it has to do with the province of Ontario.
-it was Canadian literature and the illustrations were entirely of interest to the western people-wheat fields, threshing operations, cattle ranches-there was nothing to indicate the diversity of opportunity that exists in Canada for people who want to come here. I hope we have taken some steps to cure that, even at expense of the province.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Will my hon. friend
allow one question?

No, I do not want to be interrupted. I do not mean to answer discourteously, but my hon. friend will talk about Quebec, and I do not know anything about that province. I am talking about Ontario.
Mr. LaVERGNE : I was only going to say I would be more interested in my hon. friend's opinion than in any opinion expressed by Mr. Ferguson.

My opinion is that we
would be better off if we followed the Prims Minister's policy and kept Canada for Canadians, shutting out all immigrants. That is what should have been done years ago, and that is what would have been done if it had not been for the propaganda of the Tory party. According to the London Advertiser of July 24, 1930, I find that the province of Ontario spent the following sums in inducing immigrants to come to this country:
1925		 $124,225
1926		 165,830
1927		 167,056
1928		 171,129
Who spent that money?

The province of Ontario
spent it, and in 1929 Ontario spent $181,049 to induce immigrants to come to this country. Just one year after that, in 1930, Mr. Ferguson, who had been spending the taxes of the people of Ontario to induce immigrants to come to this country, and who maintained an office in London for that purpose, went up and down this province protesting against all the people who had been brought into the country.
What did you do?

No one is a better judge of jokes than my hon. friend on the other side. But let me tell the hon. gentleman who interjected that question that when the statement was made that we had room here for thousands of Britishers, I took it upon myself to point out, although it was a matter on which the Minister of Immigration should have made a statement, that this propaganda was not in the interests of the country or in the interests of the immigrants themselves, because when they came here and were unable to find employment they became dissatisfied, and someone had to take care of them. If they went back home they told of the hardships they had met in Canada; and I pointed out, as I have said, that this was not in the best interests either of Canada or of human beings coming to the country.
Let me read certain extracts to show what my position was. The Evening Standard of London, England, in its issue of July 28, 1928, made the following statement:
Canada Closed to Miners. Trade Union Manifesto Speaks of "Misleading Propaganda."
There is no opening in Canada for the 200,000 British miners who are declared to be surplus to the home industry.
This point is emphasized in a manifesto issued by the Canadian Trades Labour Congress.
The manifesto states:-"Too long has the Canadian government remained silent and allowed misleading propaganda as to opportunities for employment in Canada to continue without any official contradiction.
"The statement by Mr. Peter Heenan, Canadian Minister of Labour, that the records show a surplus at the coal mines already in Canada should give the quietus to those who seek to exploit the misery of the British miners by seeking to induce them to emigrate to Canada."
Following that statement, the great glorified agent of the Tory party, the Montreal Gazette, had this to say in an editorial in its issue of Thursday, July 26, 1028:
Mr. Heenan to the Rescue
The Canadian government's answer to British parliamentary criticism of Canadian immigration restrictions comes from Hon. Peter
365S
Supply-Immigration

Heenan, Minister of Labour. That the Minister of Labour should be speaking for the Minister of Immigration and Colonization is significant in itself. It has been realized long enough in Canada that the voice of the Canadian government in immigration matters has been nothing more, or better, than a rebroadcast of the voice of organized labour. The views and aims of organized labour in this connection are too well known to call for much discussion; they have been defined and proclaimed upon every convenient occasion by labour bodies and labour leaders, and they can be summed up in the one word "restriction.' That is why the operation of the Canadian immigration system in Britain has been confined to so small a field, and so barren a field. What Mr. Heenan says as to the complete absence of restrictions applicable to Britishers who are physically acceptable and willing to pay full fares to Canada is altogether beside the point, since it has nothing to do with the work of bringing over immigrants, as such, by means of assisted passages and the like.
It will 'be seen that at that time I advocated the very policy which the present Minister of Immigration is carrying out. And that is what I got from the Montreal Gazette. On December 7, 1928, the Montreal Star had something to say. I understand that this newspaper organized a soup kitchen at its own expense last winter and made capital of the fact that it was feeding a number of people in this country; and the Minister of Immigration-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The people they were
feeding were in large measure people who were brought into Canada by the government of which my hon. friend was a member.
By the propaganda of the Montreal Star and the Conservative party-

It was done by your own
government.

This is what the Montreal Star said:
There is something tragic in the contrasts which the situation offers. Canada is calling earnestly for men and women to develop her matchless resources and to build up her agriculture and industry. This Dominion needs half a million men and she could absorb that number in a single year if the same effort was put forward that was initiated in the dark days of the Great war.
These men who are out of work are ablebodied, physically strong and are trained to use their muscles through long hours.
Give us your own opinion, not the opinions of newspapers.

How many years back is
that?
What are you reading from?

Where ignorance is bliss
it is folly to be wise.

They would make admirable settlers if they could get over the difficult period of the first year of settlement. They would find new homes here if they were encouraged and given a helping hand.
The Montreal Gazette of July 26, 1928 had this to say:
Debaters in the British parliament appear to think that the Canadian government is not doing its best to secure immigrants from the old country but is giving preference to Europeans. The complaints here has been that the Canadian government has not been trying very hard to obtain immigrants anywhere.
That is the kind of propaganda we were up against during the last two or three years when your humble servant was trying to preserve Canada for Canadians, just along the line that my hon. friend from Montmagny-
Who is joshing you now?

-is advocating. The
Montreal Gazette of July 31, 1928 made this statement:
The Hon. Robert Forke, Minister of Immigration, has shown full realization and a right appreciation of the seriousness of the problem that confronts his department, and he has done all he possibly can to speed up British settlers in larger numbers. But Mr. Forke is bound by a government policy obviously influenced by the view of organized labour, openly confessed last week by the Hon. Mr. Heenan, a member of the government-that the minimum of people should only be allowed to come in until everyone in Canada is prosperous and in a job! Yet Canada has room and resources to maintain a productive population larger by millions than she has to-day.
That kind of propaganda was going on all through the British Isles. Men and women out of work were led to believe that a few of us in Canada were trying to preserve this country as a closed shop, and they preferred to believe newspaper propaganda rather than to take the word of those who were really interested in the Canadian working man. And so they came to Canada and found themselves deceived when they arrived here.
Mr. LaVERGNE: How many immigrants came in between 1900 and 1911?

I do not know, but I will give the figures later on.
Mr. LaVERGNE: It was almost two millions and a half.

If that had been, read to
the immigrants they would have stayed out.

That was published in
192S, two years before the elections. The Hamilton Spectator of November 26, 1928, contained the following:
Lord Melchett Suggests Plan Canada to Grant Land. Britain to Pay Cost
London, November 26.-A suggestion that Canada should make land grants and that Britain should finance settlement schemes on the instalment basis, is made by Lord Melchett, formerly Sir Alfred Mond, who says he would like to see a really big migration movement started which would bring out at least 100,000 people to Canada without undue hindrance.
Carried on division.

My hon. friend would like to have the item carry, but I intend to put a few more things on record before it is carried. This is the kind of propaganda indulged in by politicians, and which has been supported by politicians for the last few years.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: What politicians?
I will prove my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It conveys nothing to my mind when the hon. member says "politicians."

Politicians from the Conservative party, one member of which party is over in London representing the spirit, the voice and the soul of the government of the
day.
Who is that?
He will be back.
I hope he does come back, because I lost an asset when he left. Will my hon. friend tell me why he ran away?
He will be back.

The Port Arthur News
Chronicle, a paper in my part of the country, under date of October 1, 1928, had the following to say:
If Britishers will not come to Canada, we must look elsewhere for men and women who will come. Much of the dominion still remains to be settled. Much work has to be done.
There is work that neither Britishers or Canadians will undertake if they can find other people to perform it. Large employers of labour know this. Thus we see on the railways in extra work, foreign labour with the barest sprinkling of English speaking men among them.
At this point I want to say that that is where the railway companies come in. I refer to both companies; they love to have a surplus ' of this kind of labour in order that they may encourage work at thirty cents an hour for any number of hours they like. They want to pay a wage which will not permit of a decent standard of living. The article continues :
We see the great construction works manned by non-English men in large proportions, simply carrying out instructions issued by the few supervisors. If the Britishers would come and do the work, there would be no necessity for the bringing in of so many non-English speaking men, but they will not come, and Canada cannot cease living until the Englishmen fulfil the original idea of the intention of making Canada a colony for the settlement of Englishmen alone.
The following is from a paper in my own riding, the Rainy River Record. Under date of November 11, 1928, they had this to say:
Saturday Review (London): (The report of the Industrial Transference Board shows that there are at least 250,000 more workmen in the British Isles than can be supported by the industries of the country). The remedy in which the Industrial Transference Board see most hope is in migration to the dominions. It would like to transfer to new careers 200,000 workmen with their families, for the excess of unemployed in the coal mines alone is probably at least 200,000-not one of whom has a chance of reemployment in his old work-and the migration of 200,000 abroad is therefore not an excessive transference, nor would it be throwing on the dominions by any means the whole of our surplus population. Since the war the stream of emigration from this country abroad has almost stopped, and the emigration of even 200,000 would do little more than make ud the accumulated arrears.
In the Montreal Gazette of September 15, 1928, the following appeared:
It is largely because of the Heenan-organized labour attitude that one government after another in Canada has failed to evolve and enforce an immigration policy that will bring immigrants.
I draw this to the attention of the Minister of Immigration in the hope that the Montreal Gazette will not twist that around and say that the Gordon-organized labour attitude of one government after another in Canada has failed to bring immigrants to this country. Under date of March 10, 1928, the following appears in the Montreal Gazette:
Ottawa, March 9.-An impressive and constructive immigration program was submitted to parliament this afternoon by General A. D. McRae (Conservative, North Vancouver) in his

Supply-Immigration

contribution to the budget debate. His plan contemplates "the ultimate settlement ol 60,000,000 acres of land by some 250,000 farmers. These, with their families and the urban population whieh will be required, and the consequent developments which will follow, will add 2,000,000 new people to the prairie provinces of Canada. I propose we start out to double the present population of the west. Do this and the rest of Canada will grow and prosper.''

Why is so much of the time of the committee taken up with the useless junk which the hon. gentleman is reading? Why should the committee be held up, at a time when we are trying to get legislation passed, with a reading of numerous newspaper reports? It is absolutely useless and of no interest to the general public at large. It is a nuisance.

Now that the hon. gentleman has got that off his chest, -let me read something from the Montreal Gazette, quoting what the Toronto Mail and Empire had to say:
We are pleased to learn that General McRae, M.P., North Vancouver, who met with a serious accident in Ottawa last winter, has returned from England completely restored in health. He has for many years taken an active interest in immigration and settlement work, and shortly before his accident, presented a plan which attracted widespread attention. Briefly it was to settle three hundred thousand on fifty million acres of land at a cost of $30,000,000.
The Mail and Empire, which is a Conservative paper, goes on to say:
If, as estimated, it would add two million to our population in ten years the cost does not seem excessive. General McRae's was one of the few really constuctive plans proposed for public consideration, but unfortunately his illness prevented the discussion of it which it deserved.
I would ask the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Price) to take up the cudgels where General McRae left off, and advocate now the bringing in of 300,000 people at a cost of $30,000,000 a year to settle on useless land. I defy any hon. member on the government side of the house to get up and say that that is the policy that should be pursued in Canada. Yet they induced thousands of people in the old country to sell their little sticks of furniture and start off for this great, prosperous country of Canada, and) when they got here and could not find employment, we had the spectacle of the Conservatives going up and down this country saying: These are the people that the King government brought over.

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. MacDonald, South Cape Breton):
speechtext: Time is up.

I am sorry because I am only half through.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	I agree entirely with
what my hon. friend said, but I do not think that quoting newspapers puts the responsibility on the right people. I was in the house when I was almost alone in denouncing immigration, and I lived to see the whole Conservative apposition supporting me when I was combating the immigration policy of the Laurier government. Deeds of governments speak louder than quotations ifrom newspapers, which are not responsible to the people. Who brought the immigrants to this country? That is the question. During the Liberal regime of Sir Wilfrid Laurier three million immigrants, paid immigrants, came into this country-advertised immigration, bonused immigration, and sometimes Scandalous immigration. I recall, for instance, the North Atlantic Trading Company. I was in the house in those days, and it was precisely on one of those questions that I separated from that party. It was when the Liberal party was filling up this country with the riff-raff of continental Europe. That was the policy pursued by the Liberal party for at least ten or twelve years, and it was denounced in this house first by the hon. member for Labelle and mysel'f, then by Conservatives from Quebec, and then by the leader of the opposition, Sir Robert Borden, and the whole Conservative party. And it was defended by whom? By Mr. Sifton and Mr. Frank Oliver, then Minister of the Interior and Minister of Immigration respectively. Thus, deeds speak louder than quotations from newspapers, which may be Conservative. My hon. friend quotes the Montreal Gazette. Everybody knows that the Montreal Gazette is the Taschereau organ in the province of Quebec. I do not know that Mr. Taschereau is so much of a Conservative. It may be so, but he is not supposed to be Conservative in the eyes of my hon. friend.
I remember reading to the then Minister of Immigration in the Laurier government a list of twenty-nine new races which had been brought into Canada by the immigration policy of the Laurier government. Those were the days when we had bonused immigration, premiums on immigrants, scandals involving different companies. I remember the North Atlantic Trading Company. You could not name those people because if their names were given out in public some of them would have to commit suicide. But the present Minister of Immigration has put a stop to that policy, which was ruinous to the welfare of our

Supply-Immigration
nation and to the best traditions of both races in this country, and I think the whole house should stand up and thank him for adapting such a policy. .1 have fought the Liberal party's immigration policy for the last twenty-five years, and I have fought many a battle alone. We should look at things squarely, and say that both parties have been guilty, both parties have gone the wrong way, the Liberal party more than the other; but the Conservative party was the first to put a stop to that policy this year.

Immigration salaries and contingencies, including grants to immigration societies, women's hostels, provinces, and loans-for stock, equipment, etc., for Canadian boys, as may be authorized by the governor in council, $1,905,000.

I wish the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) had been in the Conservative party during the last two or three years, because he would have tried to stop this propaganda in the British Isles. I want to say this to him. He said that the Liberal party brought those people here. I say it was the Tory propaganda that brought those people to this country.
Mr. LaVERGNE : There was no Tory government in 1904, 1905 or 1906.
Mr, HEENAN: Let me read what the present Prime Minister said in this house in 1929.
May I ask a question?
No. You don't need to ask anything because I am not going to answer it.

Will you tell us who
brought that bunch up into the northwest that do not wear any clothes?

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. MacDonald, South Cape Breton):
speechtext: Will hon. gentlemen kindly address the chair and stop this cross-fire back and forth?

It would seem that hon.
members opposite do not like the medicine they are getting, to hear that they are responsible for bringing immigrants into this country. They have misled thousands of people and brought them to Canada to suffer misery and starvation. They do not like to be reminded of the fact that they are responsible for lowering the wages of the working men in Canada.
I shall read what the present Prime Minister said as reported in Hansard of February 11, 1929:
We have here one of the largest undeveloped areas in the world; we have a very pressing necessity for more people. There need be no misapprehension about that, notwithstanding what has been said from time to time to the contrary. It will be found that the increase of population in this country, brought about through bringing additional people in, will not only lessen unemployment for those who are now in it, but will increase all employment. Those who have studied the problems connected with the movement of people realize that instead of there being a diminution of opportunities for labour the flow of new peoples into a country means the increasing of the opportunities for those who are there as well as providing work to those who may come.
I have before me a similar statement reported in the Calgary Herald of February 1, 1929. In 1930 Mayor Webb of Winnipeg led a delegation of unemployed to this city. He and his delegation said that the reason for unemployment throughout Canada was the number of immigrants which had been brought in. Then he went back to Winnipeg and was invited to speak before the Sons of England society. His speech is reported in the Free Press of April 24, 1930. I would ask hon. members to bear in mind that this is the same gentleman who after blaming the government for bringing in too many immigrants left Ottawa, returned to Winnipeg and addressed the meeting to which I have referred, as follows:
Mayor Webb told of a fine young Englishman who was in Winnipeg looking for work. He had been sent out to this country as a result of efforts made in his home city to help young fellows anxious to try their fortunes abroad.
"That is the type of man we want in this country" explained the mayor, who expressed the hope that thousands more like him would be sent to Canada and given a fair chance to succeed when they got here.
"The best thing for this country would be the arrival of a million Britishers," declared mayor Webb.
I want to point out, without mentioning further editorials of a like character-I do not wish to burden the committee because I know that it must be very trying to hon. members opposite to listen to this repetition -that this is the kind of propaganda that the King government and this country had to submit to for the last two or three years.
I know that there were thousands of miners and other people in the British Isles who were thinking of the great opportunities which prevailed in Canada and who with the assistance of immigration societies borrowed money
Supply-Immigration

to come here. When they arrived they found conditions just as I pictured them in a public speech delivered before the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: When were those miners brought to Canada to which my hon. friend refers?
Those miners were coming over here expecting to find work when they arrived.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In what years did they come?
Continually.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: They are not coming now.
They came when the hon. member was in office.
They are coming because of the propaganda of my hon. friend and his friends.
Who brought those naked Doukhobors into the northwest? You and your government.
They are naked, too.
You don't like that, do you?
That is ancient history.
May be it is, but they are still running naked.
Why not go out and tell it to the world?
You are trying to dress it.
I believe my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) and his friends are rather excited.
What about the unemployed?
Carry on.
I think I shall. I just wish to say that-
You were a fine lot of servants for the country.

What is my hon. friend growling about,-or is he grouching? Have you a grouch, too? Does my hon. friend not like this? I know it is rather hard medicine for the Tory party to take. I wish to say to the Minister of Immigration, however, that whether he believes it or not I am trying to maintain his position. I am trying to show that when I was in a position somewhat similar to his I had to withstand the criticism of editorials throughout the country.
You are not making it any easier for the minister.

They never changed my views because I still contended there were too many immigrants brought to this country. They came because of propaganda of the Conservative party, especially the branch of the party in the province of Ontario, and the taxes of the people were paid to bring those immigrants to Canada.

Why don't you
speak out so that we can hear you?

When the minister was
willing to allow a resolution to go through to provide for the' eight hour day throughout Canada the hon. member who is now interrupting was the person who talked out the measure and thereby killed it.
Yes, after you were Minister of Labour for years and could not put it through. Now you are trying to stand up and defend it.
That might be true, too. The fact remains however that the hon. member prevented his own government from putting the measure through when they were willing that it should go through.
He is a hot wave.
He is the hon. member who undertook, after the minister had agreed-

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. MacDonald, South Cape Breton):
speechtext: I would suggest that the hon. member keep to the subject before the committee.
I am going to, and I want you to keep the hon. member opposite quiet.

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. MacDonald, South Cape Breton):
speechtext: I certainly shall. I ask the hon. member to the right kindly to keep order.
I wish to say again to the Minister of Immigration that I am heart and soul with him.
Deliver me from my friends.

I do not think, however,
that the hon. member sitting to his left is with him, or he has changed his mind within the last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Whom are you talking about?

The Minister of Railways, more particularly.

Supply-Immigration

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am wholeheartedly with him.

Well you and I are going to shake hands yet. I made a speech, Mr. Chairman, with respect to people being brought into this country, and the whole Tory party including the present Prime Minister took exception to my remarks. The Tory papers also objected. On November 22nd, 1928, the Moose Jaw Times contained this editorial:
The Montreal Gazette has been devoting considerable criticism to Hon. Peter Heenan, Minister of Labour, in connection with immigration matters. Mr. Heenan has been returning the compliment and seems to be no better pleased with The Gazette than The Gazette is with him.
To the Toronto Star there is nothing surprising about this. In coming into conflict The Gazette and the Minister of Labour are both attending to their jobs and upholding the beliefs that are within them. The Star says:
Mr. Heenan is censured by The Gazette for having said that any miner-harvester excursion next year would be contingent upon the demand for extra labour that might then exist. This does not please The Gazette and is taken as indicating a hostility to immigration, a subject which, it says, Mr. Heenan should not discuss, but should leave to Mr. Forke, Minister of Immigration. But the fact is that Mr. Heenan, as Minister of Labour, was talking of labour, not immigration, when he made the statement complained of. "Any bringing over of harvesters," said Mr. Heenan, "would be contingent upon the demand for extra labour that might then exist." No Minister of Labour could very well be attending more strictly to his own business than was Mr. Heenan when he made that statement.
1 am reading these extracts to give the minister an idea of the character of the propaganda inspired by certain interests during the last two or three years in an attempt to bring in immigrants, and, conversely, to criticize anyone who would dare take the stand the present minister has taken. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I cannot see why the minister should still desire to pass this vote to grant financial assistance to immigration agents. Consequently I move that the vote be reduced to $1.

Mr. Chairman. I would
not intervene in this discussion were it not for the fact that certain statements have been made reflecting on the capability of our high commissioner in London. We have as our representative in London the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, one of the ablest men that Canada ever produced. Undoubtedly since he has been in London he has placed Canada on the map. Never in the history of this country have we had a more capable administrator than the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, ex-
Premier of Ontario, who to-day with such distinction fills the office of High Commissioner to London.

I have a case to which I
should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Immigration; and I ask the indulgence of the committee while I explain the details. This is the case of one Joseph Gordon Smith, who was dismissed from his position as temporary immigration inspector at Pacific Highway, British Columbia. In regard to his civil service examination I might say he obtained a mark of 85 per cent on the written examination and a very fair mark on the oral examination as well, and was placed sixth on the permanent list. I asked lor the papers in connection with the case, and it is from these official records I am now giving the facts.
'Complaints started to come in from the inspector in charge there with regard to this man, but at one time it was decided that he would make a fairly good officer. I read from a report dated October 16, 1930, from division inspector F. W. Taylor to the division commissioner at Vancouver. This is with reference to Inspector J. G. Smith:
The vacancy created by the transfer of inspector McNamara back to White Rock could, I am sure, be filled temporarily at least by officer Smith; and while I realize that the department would like to deal definitely with these appointments after the person concerned has been in the service a reasonable length of time, in the ease of Mr. Smith if it is possible to have him continue at the Highway office for another few months to make up the quota of inspectors required at this port, I would recommend this action, as Mr. Smith is steadily improving in his inspectional and all-round work, and I feel reasonably sure that he will continue to do so.
So you see, Mr. Chairman, this man was progressing very well, and it looked as though he would make a fairly good officer. As I say, however, complaints started to come in with regard to his work, and the two chief complaints lodged against him were later proved to be entirely unfounded. I am going to read the first complaint made against him, and also give the real facts of the case. This is a report to Mr. A. E. Skinner under date of February 21, 1931:
Referring to Mr. Whiteley's recent report in connection with the employment of Inspector J. A. Smith wherein Mr. Whiteley makes reference to a couple of complaints in Mr. Smith's inspectional work; these complaints were inquired into at the time, the first one being made by a Mr. Louis F. Bachman, who claimed at the time he was being interviewed by Mr. Smith at the Highway that he was a Y.M.C.A. worker from Milwaukee, although he did not have any credentials to identify himself and
Supply-Immigration

very little cash for his maintenance during his contemplated somewhat lengthy stay in this province, and although the man was allowed to come forward he called at the United States consular office to ascertain why he should have been questioned so closely and on following the matter up we found that Bachman was arrested a few days later by the R.C.M.P. officials in Alberta, where on being liberated he lost no time in returning to his home in Minot, North Dakota.
That was the first complaint, which was later proved to be entirely untrue. I quote from the same report, with regard to the second complaint:
The second complaint was made by Mr. H. A. Goodhugh, who was sailing from Vancouver on the ss. Aorangi on November 12th last, and this entleman called here on the morning after eing admitted at our Highway office to complain of the indifferent manner our inspector answered his many questions with reference to certain information he was endeavouring to secure concerning Vancouver and vicinity, as this was his first trip through British Columbia and it later developed that Mr. Smith unfortunately was not familiar with the particular things "Mr. Goodhugh was asking about and when he secured the information from myself he was quite willing to overlook Mr. Smith's apparent indifferent attitude in the matter.
Those were two main complaints against Mr. Smith during the time he was temporary officer, and as I have stated they were not only proved to be unfounded and unwarranted, but I think were entirely uncalled for.
Now I should like to take uip the further reasons given for his dismissal. The first is is because of his advanced age. He is an overseas active service man, and passed with a high mark, and there is a different age limit for those men than for others. His age when he passed the examination was 51, and when he was dismissed he was 53. The second complaint is that he would never make an efficient inspector, that he had always worked as a labourer or farm hand. This is entirely untrue. He had been a chef and always had followed that line of work; he had also been a chef in the British army during the last war. The only time he worked as a labourer, or anything of the sort, was when he took up a ranch at a place called Newtonbury, but this is what the inspector says:
He has always worked as a labourer or as a farm hand, and it is very hard for a man of his calibre to step into a position of this kind at his age and be successful.
I think that complaint also is entirely unfounded. Then the inspector goes on to state that this man never had any clerical experience. As a matter of fact the temporary inspectors are never given any chance to do clerical work; all the reports were filled in

by someone else, so how can they say he has no clerical experience when he had no chance to do clerical work? Then there is another statement which I find in these official records. The inspectors says:
I am very sorry that for the past two years I have had to turn down all the temporary men but one, but I take it that the department wants efficient men appointed to the service, and I am doing my best to this end.
I ask the minister to take serious note of this statement. These men are appointed as temporary inspectors, and my information is that if they do not fit in with the other men there, it is openly stated that they have the skids put under them and out they go. One man by the name of Griffin was a temporary officer in New Westminster, and just before he was made permanent he was sent out to this port and the skids were put under him. This is not a case where one can blame any political organization; this is the fault of the officials in charge of this work. It is practically a closed corporation, and it is a common saying in that district that they can put the skids under any of the temporary inspectors and prevent them from becoming permanent officials.
Those were the most important complaints, but there is a further point which aroused the ire of myself and very many others. The officials looked around to see if they really could find a reason for dismissing this man. He was efficient in every way; he had been recommended a few months back, but ju3t before he was to be made permanent they decided it was about time to get rid of him, so what do you suppose they found against him? I should like the minister to listen to this, because the middle name of this man is the same as the minister's name, and I am sure the minister will be interested in this complaint. I now read from the report:
There are two complaints against Inspector Smith, that I may say is not that he is discourteous, but his Scotch dialect is so broad that the majority of the travelling public cannot understand him when he is trying to examine them.
Do you blame me for being hostile? This is part of the official record, and to think we have come to a time in the history of Canada when a man with a Scotch dialect is to be discriminated against! I have heard the deputy speaker refer with commendable pride to the French race, but I can tell him that the record of the Scotch is not very far behind that of the French in the building up of this country of ours. I can go back to Sir John A. Macdonald and go right down the

Supply-Immigration
list of men of Scotch extraction who have done very much for this country. I think this is a gross insult, and I ask the minister that this case be investigated. I would ask the minister to remember this: they have not put on a permanent man for over two years. There are skids put under all those who do not fit in, but this is the last straw, and I am asking in the name of common justice that this slur on Scotland be removed. I have been quoting from the official records, and the only thing that they could find against the man is his Scotch accent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The hon. member need
not fear; I will take the necessary steps to see that Scotchmen get their rights. I am told they get them anyhow. The case has not come before me, and obviously I cannot offhand go into all these various cases on the international boundary. I will look into this matter and if there has been any injustice I will see that it is attended to.

This is not a dismissal under
any political organization. The matter is more serious than that. I have here a letter from which I might quote the following:
You will be surprised to know that Joe Smith has been fired from the immigration service at the highway here under circumstances that merit some attention. The complaints have been fostered by another member of the staff, but of course the signing of the report was done by the man in charge. They complained of Smith's Scottish accent. I never thought the day would come when a Scottish accent would be a detriment in this world but more especially in Canada.
This letter is from a man who was a prospective Conservative candidate in the last provincial election, and therefore it shows that the matter is more serious than a mere political dismissal. It is high time that an investigation took place at the customs and immigration ports of British Columbia.

I wish to say a word or two in regard to this question of immigration, and I do so for the benefit of the hon. member for Montmagny, who in his speech blamed the Liberal party so severely for bringing so many immigrants into the country. According to the hon. gentleman the Liberal party was entirely to blame for all the immigrants brought into the country in the last fifteen or twenty years or more. Let me direct his attention to page 2746 of Hansard of May 22, 1929, reporting a speech made by the present Minister of Railways. That hon. gentleman was then criticizing the policy of the Liberal party in regard to immigration,
and he was attempting to show that that policy had been a failure. In his speech he said:
During the first year of Liberal rule the British immigration into Canada amounted to 47 per cent of the total immigration; last year it was 33 per cent, which shows that the British immigration is decreasing, whatever the cause may be.
The following, particularly, is what I wish to call to the attention of the hon. gentleman:
During the last four fiscal years before the war, 1911 to 1914-
Our Toiy friends were in power then, and the hon. member for Montmagny was supporting them.
-we received into Canada, 1,451,000 people.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Before the war?

The hon. gentleman was
referring to the period before the war.
During the last four years during which this government-
That is, the Liberal government.
-has been in office-
That is, from 1922 or 1923 up to the time the hon. gentleman was speaking.
-we have received exactly 501,000, or a little more than one-third of the immigration during the four years before the war.
I wish to ask the hon. member for Montmagny to sleep on that.
Mr. LaVERGNE: My hon. friend asks me to sleep on his words. It reminds me of the old days. Let me tell him something that happened under the Laurier regime, when the Liberal party was making an attempt to bring in immigrants of every description- the Salvation Army, ex-convicts, prisoners and loafers. That was during the Liberal regime. The reason for that immigration which the Laurier government wished to bring in will be found at page 6151 of Hansard of April 9, 1907. That reason was stated by Mr. Smart, then Deputy Minister of Immigration, in Liverpool. He said on that occasion that this immigration was necessary to drown the French element in Canada. I would ask my hon. friend to sleep on that.

There is an arrangement with the provinces for bringing in settlers, whereby we pay a certain proportion of the interest on the money loaned for improvements on the land. Can the minister give us some idea of what this is costing the government in New Brunswick and elsewhere?
Supply-Immigration

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That applies to what is known as the New Brunswick scheme. Five hundred families are being brought in. All but about fifty of the families have come in, and I do not think there is any possibility of further families coming forward this year. I have not the figures with regard to what is known as the tripartite agreement with New Brunswick but I should be glad to get them and give them to the hon. gentleman.

The other evening when these items were under discussion I was asking the minister a question with regard to the British Immigration and Colonization Association. I have since then received a return which gives a good deal of the information I sought. I note that this organization has brought in 5,358 boys. It has received in the past year from the government a total of 535,140.08.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is from the commencement.
The last six years.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: From the time we first took an interest in it.

I have no fault to find with the present administration with regard to this organization, but I do think that in the future the policy of the government should be to refuse to allow private organizations of this kind to bring boys to Canada. As I understand it, this organization is today on the rocks. They entered into a solemn arrangement with the government that they would supply after-care to the boys who were brought over. They have no financial resources and the responsibility for carrying on the work among these boys is left to the railroads-they were originally closely associated with the organization-and to the department itself. The Dominion government has been loaded up with a large number of boys who really are not needed in Canada. Throughout the west there are at the present time thousands of school boys who do not know where to find a job. I know something of old Ontario, and the same condition exists there. I had a letter only the other day from some people who stated that they did not know what to do with their own boys on the farm. In many cases our orphan homes are unable to place the children. I will admit that in the past many farmers got cheap labour by this means, and no doubt many boys of a fine type were

brought out. However, at the present time we have sufficient boys right here in Canada to meet our needs.
Governments in the past have been willing to enter into negotiations with associations which may have had a certain financial backing but which have not been prepared to carry out their original arrangements, and the load has been passed on to the government. This brings me to the question of deportations. There have been deported 246 of these boys, and 199 have been returned under charity arrangements. A few weeks ago I gave an illustration to the house of one particular case that had been brought to my attention, a boy who had been brought to this country under some such arrangement as this and who had gone down hill and was likely to become a criminal. He was a mere tramp, drifting about, riding on freight cars, and so on. That is positive tragedy, even when confined to one individual, but it is an appalling condition when it applies to hundreds of boys who have been brought over here and allowed to drift about from place to place. A certain number of them will get into trouble; many of them have had to be deported, and it is a very serious condition. When we were discussing the question of deportations a little while ago the minister took the ground that we had to protect ourselves. Looking back over the past ten years I find that there has been no group in this house which has stood out so solidly for protecting our Canadians against immigration as has the group in this corner.
However, when these immigrants are brought in, the least that we can do is to give them a fair chance. I know the minister is faced with the task of clearing up a lot of the mess which was left for him as a result of the policies pursued for many years, but I think we must give a certain amount of humane consideration to this matter.
May I be permitted to give one or two examples which would not come under the provisions of the bill which was under consideration earlier in the evening? The following case in a western municipality came to my attention. A man from central Europe had come to Canada four years ago with his wife and three children, the eldest of which was ten years of age. He bought a home on Montreal street in Regina, and had it paid for. Last summer he was required to put in a couple more rooms, as well as water and a sewer system. This meant debt which because of unemployment he was unable to meet. He could not borrow money on the property, and he was forced to appeal to the

Criminal Code
city. He received relief to the extent of about fifty or sixty dollars, and then an attempt was made to deport him. Fortunately strong representations were made to the city council and the municipality did not urge deportation. I have no fault to find with the department in connection with this case as they had taken no definite action when I communicated with them.

Was the eldest child a
girl or a boy?

Just at the
moment, I do not recall. I do not understand what the hon. member's question has to do with this matter.
There is so much difference.

I have not the
telegram before me, but there is nothing in the information I have which refers to that particular point. I contend that it is not fair to the people whom we have asked to come here that we should force them out of the country when they get into a little trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There was no effort made to deport that particular man.

I said distinctly
that I was not blaming the department.
Why bring that up?

We are dealing
with the immigration policy of this country, and I suggest that we are reaching the point where we are not being fair with the immigrants who have been brought here.
I have another case, in connection with which I made inquiries of the department. This man was a printer who was arrested as he was about to enter Canada after spending some time in the sanatorium of the International Typographical Union at Colorado Springs. This man, by name James Reid, was ordered to be deported, and died in New York on Friday, May 29, before the deportation order could be made effective. I was told by the department that had this case been appealed, the man probably would have been allowed to die in this country. This man had been living in the city of Toronto where his brother and sister are located; he was sent to a sanitorium and when it was found that he was not doing so well he was sent to the sanatorium at Colorado Springs. When it was obvious that he had not very much longer to live he decided to come back to die at his sister's home, but he was refused entry to Canada. I suggest that in cases of this kind a little humanity should prevail.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Wherein did the Canadian officials fail in that case?

I would say that
in a case of that kind the man should have been permitted to come back into Canada.
